Following the election of Donald Trump as the US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainties. After the new US administration takes office, the US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects — a shift from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and a shift from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. It is worth noting that the risks faced by emerging market economies have intensified amid a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar, and the possibility of the US adopting trade protectionist measures. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose in tandem with US dollar interbank interest rates. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remained benign, and overall loan growth picked up further in the second half of 2016. Following the introduction of the new stamp duty measure, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment immediately, but has rebounded recently. Looking ahead, banks should carefully assess the implications of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes and, more broadly, US policy uncertainties, particularly the risk of massive capital outflows and the potential impact on domestic interest rates. Following the election of Donald Trump as the US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainties. Not only was the election outcome unexpected by the market, but the associated market reactions were also surprising. In particular, expectations that measures such as tax reforms, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation introduced by Trump would boost US economic growth have driven global stock markets higher. After the new US administration takes office, the US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects — a shift from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and a shift from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. However, the tax cuts expected by the market under the Trump administration may fail to produce the anticipated stimulative effect on US economic growth. Especially as US economic activity is currently close to its economic potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, but would exacerbate the upside risks to US inflation. While it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (Fed) will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening as a result, long-term bond yields have risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. Meanwhile, the rise of trade protectionism would result in a "lose-lose" situation for the US and the rest of the world. An increase in trade barriers would lead to market distortions detrimental to overall interests, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Meanwhile, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the European economy where the recovery remains fragile. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows has increased due to the faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar. This could drag on economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, amid expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration and concerns over a sharp rise in energy prices, the market has repriced inflation risks, leading to a broad-based and significant increase in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. The findings suggest that since the "taper tantrum" in 2013, the impact of the US Treasury market on sovereign bond markets has deepened, and US interest rate hikes and tightening financial conditions would have significant impacts on both advanced and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016 alongside a rebound in exports, but market volatility, such as currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields in the region driven by concerns over potential policy changes by the new US administration, only gradually stabilised towards the beginning of this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain stable growth in 2017, but the risks and uncertainties it faces have increased. A US interest rate hike, currency depreciation in the region, and heightened financial market volatility could lead to a tightening of financial conditions. Meanwhile, the US may implement protectionist policies, which could affect economies in the region, although the actual impact remains unclear at present. In Mainland China, overall economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016, supported by solid growth in infrastructure investment and an improvement in private sector business spending. Although the economy continues to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainties remain over the Mainland's growth outlook. In particular, with the government's determination to curb rising housing prices, the real estate sector's contribution to growth this year may decline if the property market continues to cool. Meanwhile, the ongoing economic restructuring and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainties surrounding the near-term economic outlook. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 alongside the appreciation of the US dollar and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private sector economic activity, there remain some concerns in the market regarding the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given that M1 growth has accelerated while M2 growth has slowed. Box 2 (see page 24) explores whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) examines the factors that may have led to the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings indicate no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and the main reasons for M1 growing significantly faster than M2 are that monetary easing in recent years has reduced the opportunity cost of holding liquid money, and rising economic uncertainties may have increased the demand for precautionary money. Hong Kong's economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while robust infrastructure activities in the fourth quarter drove investment growth. Externally, goods export growth rose alongside an improvement in regional trade flows, while services exports grew steadily in tandem with the recovery in trade-related and transportation services. Due to faster growth in imports of goods and services, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. With the pick-up in economic growth, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. The government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2-3% and 2.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook still faces significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has increased downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong's external demand. With the US dollar facing appreciation pressure and expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to provide less support to the real economy, which could lead to a tightening of domestic financial conditions, particularly if tail risks materialise. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of a Financial Conditions Index for Hong Kong to help monitor domestic financial conditions. Since the second half of 2016, domestic inflationary pressures have remained moderate, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum picked up slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly driven by volatile food prices and rising housing rentals. With stable import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, but weakened occasionally following the US interest rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. Along with the appreciation of the US dollar, the nominal effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar rose further. Due to the large Monetary Base, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained low, but have risen since October driven by year-end funding demand and catching up with US interest rate hikes. Consequently, the average mortgage rate, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage lending business, edged up to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with 2.2% in the first half. The growth was supported by stronger domestic economic activity and increased financing demand from multinational corporations towards the year-end. Domestic loan growth picked up slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a small decline in the first half of the year. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans recorded a growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans. The funding position of banks remained broadly sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting that deposit growth outpaced loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 59.9% at the end of the year, and the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio dropped significantly to 63.8% due to strong growth in US dollar deposits. Due to the strong US dollar, both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool (comprising customer deposits and outstanding certificates of deposit) consolidated further along with other offshore renminbi markets, and the volatility of offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates increased significantly. Nevertheless, banks' renminbi liquidity management remained robust, and the average daily turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is likely to continue facing headwinds from uncertainties over the renminbi exchange rate movements. Along with the improvement in global market conditions, the Hong Kong stock market closed significantly higher during the reporting period. Although the US presidential election yielded an unexpected outcome, the market experienced only a brief shock. This was mainly due to investors' expectations of fiscal stimulus measures by the Trump administration, which drove global stock markets higher. While benefiting from this, the local market remained cautious amidst optimism, possibly due to concerns over a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges to the Mainland's economic outlook, uncertainties in renminbi policies, and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuation could provide support to the market. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply towards the end of last year and the yield spread against US Treasuries widened rapidly, the Hong Kong dollar bond market continued to expand steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi bond market recovered in the second half of 2016 after contracting in the first half, but new bond issuance for the whole year still recorded a decrease compared to the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier search-for-yield investment strategies, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets will face pressure. As US trade policies remain unclear and the renminbi exchange rate may remain volatile, the outlook for these two bond markets over the next six months will continue to be clouded by significant uncertainties. Following the government's introduction of the new stamp duty measure, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment immediately, but has rebounded recently. In view of renewed market exuberance, the government raised the stamp duty to a flat rate of 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets fell in the subsequent two months. However, transaction volumes have risen recently, partly reflecting developers' increased launches of primary market projects. Meanwhile, property prices continued to rise to new highs, although the upward momentum has moderated.

Following Donald Trump's unexpected election as US President, uncertainty regarding US policies has increased. Although market focus is centered on the short-term benefits brought by potential large-scale fiscal policies and pro-business measures, US economic activity is currently close to its economic potential; fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, but will further exacerbate the upside risks to inflation. More importantly, the risks faced by emerging market economies are increasing along with the capital outflow pressures brought by the accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while potential trade protectionist measures by the US will also threaten global trade flows. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and recent export volumes have also increased. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, US dollar appreciation, and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are expected to remain volatile, and the downside risks to economic growth are rising. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated marginally in the second half of 2016, supported by resilient infrastructure investment growth and improved private sector business spending. The Mainland economy continues to rebalance, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, but the ongoing advancement of economic structural adjustments and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the short-term economic outlook. Given the government's determination to curb rising housing prices, if the property market continues to cool, the real estate sector's contribution to economic growth this year may also decrease. On the external front, although the RMB remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased at the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, and subsequently appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Following Trump's unexpected election as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly, particularly as market expectations that Trump's implementation of tax reforms, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending, and deregulation policies would boost US economic growth and inflation, stimulating a rally in major stock markets (Chart 2.1). Consequently, market expectations for US inflation and US interest rate hikes escalated, causing US Treasury yields to surge and the US dollar to strengthen. Chart 2.1 Stock market indices of selected advanced economies. However, the Trump tax cuts anticipated by the market may fail to generate the positive impact on US economic growth expected by the market. Although shifting economic policy to rely on fiscal easing measures would help alleviate the heavy burden borne by monetary easing policies, given the current stage of the US economic cycle, whether now is the appropriate time to implement fiscal easing measures is debatable. Although the pace of US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap is gradually narrowing, and the February unemployment rate also matched the Federal Reserve's estimated natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, reflecting that US economic activity is already close to its economic potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, and the fiscal multiplier will be lower than during a recession (for example, see Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012)) 1. In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve indicate that tax cuts on labor or capital could lead to a reduction in tax revenues (for example, see Trabandt and Uhlig (2012)) 2. In any case, with diminishing excess capacity, any further measures to boost economic growth, even if their real impact on economic growth is limited, could push up inflation. At the same time, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionist measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, could also exacerbate the upside risks to US inflation. Even with the increased risk of rising US inflation, the Federal Reserve remains cautious about tightening US monetary policy and leans towards maintaining an ultra-loose monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have already risen, partly reflecting the increased US inflation risks. Since the US election, although market forecasts for the future federal funds rate have been revised upwards to near the Federal Reserve's median projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Federal Reserve's longer-run projections (Chart 2.2). Therefore, an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes could trigger the risk of significant market volatility. While financial markets are focused on the short-term benefits of stronger US economic growth driven by potential expansionary fiscal policies and pro-business measures, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further rise in US national debt. Indeed, the Trump administration may fulfill its campaign promises by adopting trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Future federal funds rate projections: Federal Reserve and the market. In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and headwind to the European economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the Eurozone is gradually improving, with real GDP growing moderately by 1.7% year-on-year in the fourth quarter, only slightly lower than the 1.8% year-on-year increase in the third quarter, compared to the stronger recovery of the US economy, economic activity in the Eurozone remains only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels (Chart 2.3). Since the Brexit decision last summer, the market has been concerned about the eventual breakup of the Eurozone. Although Italy's economic and political situation appears to have stabilized following the formation of a new government and the implementation of banking sector rescue measures, against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment, the upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) could become political flashpoints. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, European sovereign bond yields have continued to climb, and corporate bond spreads have also widened; this situation is particularly evident in peripheral countries, potentially creating a vicious cycle for the real economy and exerting pressure on real business investment in the Eurozone. Chart 2.3 Real GDP of major advanced economies. In Japan, real GDP has been revised upwards in recent quarters, with the annualized growth rate increasing to 1.6% year-on-year in the fourth quarter of 2016, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger economic recovery than previously expected. However, partly due to structural issues in the labor market, wage growth has been slow, leading to sluggish consumption growth. At the same time, the recent rapid depreciation of the Japanese yen implies that the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation caused by the earlier yen appreciation is about to start fading. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicates an improvement in the short-term inflation outlook, and although "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) fell to 0.1% in December, it is expected to bottom out and rebound. Nevertheless, facing long-term and structural headwinds, growth is likely to remain slow, and inflation expectations remain at around 0.5% – 0.6%, lower than the levels when Abenomics was introduced in early 2014; therefore, the risk that the inflation rate will fail to reach the Bank of Japan's medium-term target of 2% still exists. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits brought by faster US economic growth through trade channels may be smaller, as the US has reduced imports since the global financial crisis and may implement protectionist policies. Meanwhile, the accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar will lead to a tightening of financial conditions, exacerbating downside risks to the economy. This could drag down economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, coupled with concerns over surging energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risks, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across the board in advanced economies as well as many emerging market economies. Box 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia 3, real economic activity has recently regained momentum, with regional GDP growing modestly and inflation rising. real GDP growth — In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable due to steady private consumption in several regional economies. At the same time, exports generally rose slightly from their 2015 lows. This benefited not only from the stabilization of China's growth but also from the improved performance of advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters (such as Malaysia and Indonesia), the rebound in commodity prices also provided an additional boost. Other major exporters (such as South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) also regained upward momentum due to growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — With the rebound in commodity (especially oil) prices, producer price inflation generally showed an upward trend. Although this will push up industrial costs or even consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may increase due to the decline in long-term deflation risks. Accelerated producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation; the actual impact depends on the extent to which the increase in producer prices is passed on to consumer prices, which varies across economies. Consensus forecasts for the Consumer Price Index indicate that although inflation in several regional economies will remain slightly below their respective central banks' 2017 inflation targets, it will rise closer to the target levels (Chart 2.4). With the exception of Indonesia, central banks in the East Asian region generally maintained their accommodative monetary policies with unchanged interest rates; Indonesia cut interest rates twice in September and October last year to boost growth. Chart 2.4 Headline CPI inflation, forecasts, and central bank targets in the East Asian region. Despite the improvement in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 caused short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign exchange markets — Following the US presidential election, investors expected US inflation to rise, and most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies have depreciated to a lesser extent or even appreciated slightly since the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Spot foreign exchange depreciation against the US dollar and changes in nominal effective exchange rates since the US election. Bond and stock markets — Asset prices briefly declined following the US presidential election but quickly stabilized. The spreads between sovereign bonds of East Asian economies and US Treasury bonds widened. However, as markets stabilized, yields in some regional economies declined, though they have not yet returned to pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, the spreads have narrowed compared to pre-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads between 10-year sovereign bonds and US Treasury bonds. Portfolio investment flows — Portfolio investment funds flowed out of the East Asian region in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "taper tantrum" in mid-2013. By the first few weeks of 2017, capital inflows were recorded again, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, growth in the region is expected to remain stable, but the pace will still be lower than the historical average. Due to rising uncertainties regarding US government policies and the potential policy responses by the Federal Reserve, financial markets are highly likely to remain volatile. A significant rise in the US dollar and yields could attract funds to flow from the region to the US, causing investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, which is particularly concerning for assets with currently high valuations. The tightening of financial conditions under such circumstances would also put repayment pressure on corporations with large amounts of US dollar-denominated debt. Macroeconomically, a general global increase in interest rates would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, which not only drags down aggregate demand in the short term but may also affect potential growth in the long term. Finally, exporting countries in the region face the potential threat of trade protectionist policies implemented by the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Chart 2.7), especially in the region's major export industries, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, clothing, and textiles. Over the past two decades, US imports in these industries have increased, resulting in massive job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalizing US manufacturing could pose significant risks to exporting countries in the region.

Accelerated growth in private consumption and robust building and construction activities in the public sector drove a slight acceleration in Hong Kong's economic growth in the second half of 2016. Due to an increasingly uncertain external environment, economic growth is expected to be moderate in 2017. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflation pressures are expected to remain contained. Hong Kong's economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer sentiment and stable labor market conditions, the growth of private consumption accelerated, becoming the main driver of GDP growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at the Hong Kong International Airport, building and construction activities also became robust. However, weak corporate capital expenditure narrowed the contribution of overall investment spending to GDP growth. Externally, both exports and imports of goods accelerated in tandem with rising regional trade flows (Chart 3.2). 22 Trade-related and transportation services drove further growth in service exports, while service imports rebounded partly due to strong travel demand from local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports The labor market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at 3.4% in the first three quarters, and then edged down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, the unemployment rates in several major sectors declined during the second half of the year, including the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors, partly because the slowdown in the retail sector stabilized. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labor force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, due to the uncertain global macroeconomic and financial environment, global economic and trade growth may remain moderate. Coupled with the strong US dollar leading to an increase in the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar, this will constrain Hong Kong's export performance. On the domestic front, although stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, dragged down by rising interest rates, private consumption is expected to grow moderately. With the increase in housing supply and the rollout of multiple infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should grow steadily, but subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will suppress corporate capital expenditure. The government currently forecasts real GDP growth for 2017 to be between 2% and 3%, while the average forecast by private sector analysts is 2.0%. The economic growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly those stemming from the external environment. Policy uncertainties of the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, and potential protectionist trade policies could pose headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and elections in several major European countries may also lead to asset market volatility and affect Hong Kong dollar fund flows. Furthermore, the normalization of US interest rates will tighten domestic monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, although domestic inflation has seen an uptick in quarter-on-quarter momentum in recent months, it has remained moderate overall. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The annualized 3-month rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before edging down to 2.4% in January. The rise in inflation momentum was mainly driven by higher prices of tradable goods and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, tradable goods inflation rose from a negative figure in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by the prices of basic foodstuffs and clothing and footwear. Meanwhile, since the third quarter, with the narrowing decline in private housing rentals and the upward adjustment of public housing rentals in September 2016, the housing rental component of the CCPI increased, but subsequently moderated slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major components Chart 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rentals In the short term, due to weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflation pressures are expected to remain contained. As the strong Hong Kong dollar offsets the impact of the rebound in global commodity prices to a certain extent, imported inflation will remain low (Chart 3.7). Domestically, the output gap was estimated to remain close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures and thereby restrain inflation in the services components. Despite a tight labor market, wage increases have been mild in recent quarters; real payroll per person engaged rose by 1.1% in the first half of 2016, and then fell by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). The external environment remains persistently uncertain, leading to cautious business sentiment. Against this backdrop, the increase in labor costs should be contained. In addition, due to the sluggish retail sales performance in recent months, the increase in retail property rentals is expected to be moderate. Furthermore, the impact of the earlier softening in private housing rentals will gradually surface, which will also help alleviate inflation pressures. It is expected that, overall, the year-on-year inflation rate for the whole year of 2017 will decline; the government forecasts the underlying inflation rate for the year to be 2.0%, lower than the 2.3% in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labor costs and real payroll per person engaged The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside risks, if inflation accelerates under the Trump administration in the US, it may lead to a faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, which could push up domestic mortgage rates and increase downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. Meanwhile, the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar may keep import prices weak and simultaneously weaken the city's attractiveness to inbound tourists. On the upside risks, if the global economic expansion is faster than expected, it may accelerate Hong Kong's economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby bringing upward pressure on domestic inflation. In addition, the upwardly adjusted statutory minimum wage will take effect on May 1, 2017, which may cause inflation to rise further, but the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed on to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose in tandem with US dollar interbank rates. Driven partly by the improving local economic environment, overall loans continued to grow moderately. Looking ahead, the volatility of Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalization, unclear policy directions of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe. Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November caused Asian currencies to fall generally, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained stable. However, the interest rate projections announced by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on December 13-14, 2016, fueled market expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened somewhat in tandem with other Asian currencies, but as market expectations for a US interest rate hike in March rose from mid-February, the Hong Kong dollar began to show signs of weakening. During the reporting period, the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund flow indicators Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators Along with the strong US dollar, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar rose by 4.9% between August and December, before stabilizing recently (Chart 4.3). As the impact of the narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was mild, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar closely tracked the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-resident portfolio investment in equity and debt securities recorded net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and a large number of initial public offering activities (Table 4.A). However, driven partly by Hong Kong banks increasing their holdings of US debt securities, resident portfolio investment in debt securities recorded massive outflows, which more than offset the inflows from non-residents. Consequently, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds indicated that portfolio investment outflows occurred in the last quarter of 2016, mainly because the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election, coupled with expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, put pressure on the local financial market and other Asian markets (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data showed that Hong Kong portfolio investment faced fund inflow pressures in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to investors' optimism about the US adopting expansionary fiscal policies, which improved the performance of global financial markets. Chart 4.4 Market survey on equity and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, the volatility of Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. If the pace of US interest rate normalization accelerates, it will increase the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. Meanwhile, amid uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process, and elections in EU member states, fund flows may experience increased volatility. In addition, increased investment demand for Hong Kong dollar assets from Mainland investors may exert fund inflow pressures on the Hong Kong dollar. Even though the northbound trading volume exceeded the southbound trading volume in the initial period following the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment fund flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained massive and rose further by 1.7% in the second half of the year, driven by the growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the Aggregate Balance and the total amount of outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes broadly remained at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Within this total, due to the additional issuance of HK$49.0 billion of Exchange Fund Bills to meet banks' strong demand for liquidity management, the Aggregate Balance shrank while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes rose correspondingly. Chart 4.5 Components of the monetary base As the local economy gradually firmed up, the pace of Hong Kong dollar money supply growth accelerated. The growth of the Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded a faster growth of 6.6% in the second half of the year (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by increased transaction demand stemming from stronger local economic activities and a rebound in initial public offering activities. Analyzed by counterpart assets, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks' net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which represented money created from credit expansion and net Hong Kong dollar fund inflows from the non-bank private sector, respectively. Chart 4.6 Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in its counterpart assets On the other hand, the growth of foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After growing by 10.2% in the first half of the year, US dollar deposits recorded a higher increase of 12.8% in the second half amid the strong US dollar (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted further by 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, the growth of total deposits with authorized institutions rose to 6.2% in the second half of 2016, while the full-year growth was 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Driven by expectations of US interest rate normalization, banks' wholesale funding costs rose in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained low, they increased somewhat, driven partly by year-end funding demand and the catch-up with the rise in US dollar interbank rates. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by 54 and 46 basis points to 0.66% and 1.02% respectively in the second half of the year (Chart 4.8). Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards in tandem with the US dollar yield curve, with the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rising by about 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at the end of December. Entering early 2017, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally fell due to reduced funding demand, while long-term Hong Kong Government Bond yields also declined slightly along with US Treasury yields. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates and 10-year Government Bond yields Due to the massive deposit base of the banking system, the increase in retail-level interest rates was relatively small. Banks' average funding costs (as measured by the composite interest rate) remained at a low level, edging up by only 6 basis points from seven months ago to 0.32% in January 2017 (Chart 4.9). Due to relatively stable funding costs and intensified competition in the mortgage loan business, the average interest rate on newly approved mortgage loans fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017 in tandem with the rise in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates. Chart 4.9 Composite interest rate and average interest rate on newly approved mortgage loans Looking ahead, the upward pace of local interest rates will depend on the speed of US interest rate normalization, the scale of fund outflows, and global macro-financial developments. The upward pressure on local interest rates, coupled with the rise in the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar along with the US dollar, may reduce the support of local financial conditions to the real economy. Box 4 discusses the compilation of the Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index for monitoring local financial conditions. Driven by stronger local economic activities and rising cross-border funding demand, overall loans rose further by 4.2% in the second half of the year, following a 2.2% growth in the first half (Chart 4.10). With rising economic growth momentum, local loan growth accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half of the year to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half of the year after a slight decline in the first half, partly reflecting the increased year-end funding demand of multinational corporations. Analyzed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half of the year, and foreign currency loans also recorded a moderate growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans. For 2016 as a whole, overall loans grew moderately by 6.5%, compared with 3.5% in 2015. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Analyzed by economic sector, the performance of local loans was mixed in the second half of the year (Chart 4.11). Loans to financial concerns and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half of the year, reflecting to some extent the strong funding demand driven by the better growth prospects of these sectors. Loans for building, construction, and property development also accelerated in growth along with increased private construction activities. On the other hand, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade financing and loans to the manufacturing, wholesale, and retail sectors declined. Chart 4.11 Local loan growth in selected sectors The growth of household debt accelerated to 4.3% in the second half of the year, compared with 0.5% in the first half. Within household debt, partly reflecting the improving economic environment, personal loan (including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes) rose by 7.2% (Chart 4.11), and the growth of residential mortgage loans accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting the buoyant residential property transactions between July and October. Consequently, the household debt-to-GDP ratio also rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Household debt-to-GDP ratio and its components Banks' funding conditions remained broadly stable. Reflecting that deposit growth outpaced loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down from 78.2% at the end of June 2016 to 77.1% at the end of the year (Chart 4.13); Meanwhile, the overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 61.4% to 59.9% at the end of the year, within which the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio dropped significantly to 63.8% due to strong US dollar deposit growth. Chart 4.13 Loan-to-deposit ratios Due to expectations of rising interest rates and the rapidly changing macro-financial environment, credit growth will face uncertainties in the period ahead. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook showed that loan demand remained soft in the near term. Due to the appreciation of the US dollar, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened (Chart 4.14). The offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi exchange rate for most of the latter part of 2016, and closed at an intra-year low of 6.98 against the US dollar at the end of 2016. The offshore renminbi interbank market experienced renewed liquidity tightening pressures in December, partly reflecting the deterioration in financial market conditions and banks' precautionary funding demand towards the year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased their liquidity buffers amid worsening market sentiment, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate once surged to 61.3% on January 6, 2017. The rise in offshore renminbi funding costs subsequently led to the unwinding of short offshore renminbi positions, driving a rebound in the offshore renminbi exchange rate in early January 2017, and the spread between the offshore and onshore renminbi also turned into a premium. Since mid-January, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have stabilized somewhat, and liquidity conditions have gradually improved, with the overnight and three-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates falling to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively at the end of February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared to the same period in 2015, driven by growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment allowances. The capital positions and asset quality of banks also remained sound. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose significantly following the US interest rate hike in December, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust. The funding costs of retail banks remained stable and at low levels, supported by a large retail deposit base. However, banks should carefully assess the impact of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, particularly the risk of substantial capital outflows and their subsequent potential impact on local interest rates. Furthermore, given the continuous rise in the leverage levels of non-local corporates, a sharp increase in interest rates could lead to a deterioration in banks' asset quality. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong banks against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio requirement will be increased to 1.875% effective from 1 January 2018. The profitability of retail banks improved, with the return on assets rising from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 (red line in Chart 5.1). The improvement in profitability was driven by growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a decrease in loan impairment allowances. For the full year of 2016, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose from 1.05% for the full year of 2015 to 1.10%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks continued to improve, reaching 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Wholesale funding costs in Hong Kong rose significantly following the resumption of US interest rate hikes in December 2016. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR increased notably by 33 basis points in December 2016, although it remained at a low level by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates However, the overall impact of the US interest rate hike on the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) funding costs of retail banks remained mild. This is because the primary funding source for retail banks is retail deposits, and even with the interest rate hike, retail deposit rates remained stable and at low levels. Under these circumstances, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average HKD funding cost of retail banks, edged up by only 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016, after hovering at a low level of around 0.26% for more than a year. On a broader level, a similar situation was observed in the total HKD and US dollar (USD) funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. Although banks' average HKD and USD funding costs in the non-deposit market rose by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, the increase in the average deposit funding costs in the retail market was smaller, rising by only 11 basis points. Overall, the average total HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks increased by 17 basis points (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD funding costs and maturity of licensed banks The magnitude and pace of the increase in HIBOR exceeded those of the funding costs of Hong Kong banks, which may benefit some retail banks. This is because they have actively promoted HIBOR-based mortgage loans over the past few years, and the rise in interest rates on such loans may help widen their overall net interest margins. However, the improvement in net interest margins may be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In fact, there are signs that some banks have reduced the spread of their mortgage rates over the benchmark and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. In the longer term, as the US is expected to raise interest rates further, banks may soon face upward pressure on retail deposit rates, thereby affecting their funding costs and exerting a more significant impact on net interest margins. The capitalization of banks remained strong and well above the international minimum requirements. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) remained at a high level of 19.2% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio was 16.4%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Meanwhile, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions also remained stable at 51.0%. Both ratios remained well above their respective statutory minimum requirements, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks arising from potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. During the reporting period, the asset quality of retail banks' loan portfolios remained sound. At the end of December 2016, the classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio remained at low levels of 0.72% and 0.53%, respectively. Both ratios remained low by historical standards (Chart 5.10). Banks' expectations for short-term credit growth were mixed. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2016 showed that, although the majority of the surveyed AIs expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, the proportion of surveyed AIs expecting an increase in loan demand over the next three months rose slightly to 14% (Table 5.A). In the second half of 2016, the credit risk of unsecured personal loans remained manageable, with the annualized credit card charge-off ratio and delinquent ratio declining to 1.92% and 0.24% respectively at the end of December (Chart 5.11). However, the debt-servicing ratio (DSR) 47 for new mortgages rose from 44.0 in the second quarter of 2016 to 48.8 in the fourth quarter (red line in Chart 5.12), mainly reflecting an increase in the average amount of new mortgage loans (Chart 5.13). The continued normalization of US interest rates may further increase the personal debt burden. A sensitivity test shows that, assuming a 300-basis-point increase in interest rates with other factors held constant, the ratio could rise significantly to 67.3 within four quarters. 48 Banks should remain vigilant against the risks associated with the continuous rise in the personal debt burden.
