As the market reassessed US inflation risks, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. In February, global stock markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, completely wiping out the significant gains made early in the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The sustained rally in global stock markets amid low volatility over the past two years was driven by market expectations that the ideal economic environment of steady growth, low inflation, and low interest rates would continue. However, these expectations are now facing risks from tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionism sentiment, and geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but the market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall loans continued to increase, albeit at a slower pace. Property price growth and transaction volumes both rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017 after experiencing a slight slowdown in the middle of the year. Looking ahead, the return of volatility in global and local financial markets may add volatility to fund flows in Hong Kong. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, as well as the ongoing normalization of US monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant against increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflow risks. Especially, given the continuous rise in corporate leverage and the high level of personal debt burdens, banks should assess the potential impact of higher-than-expected interest rate hikes on asset quality. Following the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) hovering at low levels for more than two years, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global stock markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index plunging by more than 10% at one point, completely offsetting the significant gains recorded in early January. Market sentiment shifted due to signs that the global economic recovery might exert upward pressure on long-subdued US wages and prices, which could in turn lead the Federal Reserve to accelerate its pace of interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rally in global stock markets over the past two years was built on market expectations that economic conditions would remain ideal. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activities in both advanced and emerging market economies picking up synchronously. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform bill, which included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and individual tax codes, raising market hopes that the robust US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the strengthening activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained mild, further consolidating market expectations that global interest rates would stay low for a prolonged period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rose significantly in 2017, with US stock markets in particular repeatedly hitting new highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global stock markets reassessed inflation risks. After the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has now reached its output potential, and the expected cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts may accelerate the rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy more quickly. At the same time, as tax cuts will lead to a higher fiscal deficit, the US may issue more Treasury bonds in the future, a move expected to increase upward pressure on long-term bond yields while the Federal Reserve continues to advance its balance sheet normalization. Outside the US, strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led to market expectations that their central banks may scale back their quantitative easing programs. If implemented, this would lead to a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks triggered by international political and geopolitical tensions could also cloud the global economic growth outlook. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminum. These moves raise concerns about whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, should geopolitical tensions escalate unexpectedly, it could affect global trade and exacerbate volatility in global financial markets. Given these uncertainties in the global economic outlook, it is questionable whether the current high valuations in global asset markets can be sustained. Fundamentally, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical growth in global demand and the expected rise in the fiscal deficit due to US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R\*); coupled with the expectation that the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalization will lead to a higher term premium, this may drive up long-term interest rates, thereby adversely affecting asset market valuations. In East Asia, regional economies are also in an ideal environment of steady growth and mild inflation. Along with sound economic performance and an optimistic outlook, capital inflows have accelerated, and financial markets have rallied concurrently. However, this favorable outlook faces downside risks from various factors: tightening global liquidity caused by the synchronized normalization of monetary policies by major central banks; the inward-looking trade policies pursued by the US government; geopolitical tensions; and the potential tightening of offshore US dollar liquidity as US corporations repatriate profits on a large scale in response to the one-time "deemed repatriation" provision under the country's tax reform. Any shocks to credit and financial markets could trigger a reversal of capital flows, and highly leveraged sectors and economies are the most vulnerable to the impact of tightening financial conditions. Regarding Mainland China, supported by steady consumption, robust infrastructure, and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year, the Mainland Chinese economy performed well in the second half of 2017. Meanwhile, signs of the rise of the "new economy" have become increasingly apparent, with sectors such as high value-added manufacturing and services demonstrating strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist. In particular, the extent to which the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressures on growth posed by the further advancement of structural reforms remains to be seen. Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to adopt a proactive fiscal policy stance, which may help mitigate adverse economic developments if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. In particular, following the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in tier-1 cities. Meanwhile, as banks tightened their loan approval standards, their risk exposures to enterprises in industries with overcapacity remained under control, and shadow banking activities also slowed down amid financial deleveraging. In addition to the above positive developments, our analysis also indicates that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. Especially, borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capabilities appear to have tightened, possibly due to weakened support provided by local governments (for details, please refer to Box 2 on page 28). On the external front, amid stabilizing economic conditions and subsiding risks, capital outflow pressures remained mild for most of 2017. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for the whole of 2017, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Supported by favorable employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017. Overall investment spending also rebounded due to an increase in corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, benefiting from the improved growth in global trade and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance further improved. Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods remained a drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. Among the components, private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports will continue to support economic growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. The Government and market consensus forecast real GDP growth for 2018 to be between 3% and 4%, and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the aforementioned external environment, Mainland China's economic performance under tightening financial conditions, and the trajectory of the local asset market. Although the unemployment rate fell to a near 20-year low of 2.9%, local inflation pressures remained contained. However, quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum has shown signs of a slight pickup in recent months. Within this, prices of both tradables and services increased. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up slightly to a still-mild level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of rising rentals for newly signed private residential leases. Driven by funding demand from IPO activities and seasonal funding needs, liquidity conditions tightened, and the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions increased, prompting the spot Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities revived, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened again from December 2017 onwards. In early 2018, despite turbulence in global financial markets (especially stock markets), the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) faced upward pressure between September and December 2017. This was mainly driven by funding demand from IPO activities and banks' prudent approach to liquidity management approaching the year-end. In December, the average overnight and 3-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points from six months ago to 0.25% and 1.26%, respectively. After easing slightly in early January 2018, HIBORs remained broadly stable and were unaffected by the recent correction in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average interest rate for newly approved mortgage loans by banks tracked the rise in short-term HIBORs, increasing to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banks' funding costs remained generally low after a brief spike in October due to IPO activities, with the composite interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure; if global financial market sentiment shifts abruptly, the volatility of fund flows may increase. For the whole of 2017, total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1%. Following a strong growth of 10.2% in the first half of the year, loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half. Among them, the growth rates of domestic loans across most sectors and loans for use outside Hong Kong both declined. The growth of foreign currency loans slowed, partly due to rising US dollar funding costs. Meanwhile, driven by the favorable local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to record rapid growth. As Hong Kong dollar loans grew faster than deposits, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% at year-end, the highest level since March 2015. On the other hand, due to the relatively slow growth of foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at year-end. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilization between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December onwards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool (comprising total renminbi customer deposits and outstanding certificates of deposit), after a slight decline in the first half of the year, rebounded slightly in the second half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi business, although renminbi loans continued to decline, the amount of renminbi trade settlement handled by banks in Hong Kong rebounded in the second half of the year. The average daily turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road initiative and the continued internationalization of the renminbi.

The synchronized strengthening momentum of the global economy since late 2016 has shown no signs of abating. The improved growth outlook drove global stock markets consistently higher in 2017 and early 2018. However, as the market reassessed US inflation risks, global stock markets experienced a sell-off and significant volatility in February, marking the end of the tranquility seen in financial markets over the past two years. Looking ahead, the risk of tightening global financial conditions, along with a series of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. Amid a tight labor market, US tax cuts could accelerate the cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to quicken its pace of monetary policy tightening. As the Federal Reserve continues to advance its balance sheet normalization, the increased issuance of US Treasuries to finance tax cuts may add upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The looming shadow of rising trade barriers and any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could also pose a threat to the nascent recovery in global trade. In East Asia, benefiting from strong export performance and stable domestic demand, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017. However, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it also faces various downside risks, such as a potentially sharper-than-expected tightening of global monetary conditions, inward-looking US trade policies, and geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialize, they would also increase the risk of capital flow reversals. Policymakers are facing multiple challenges: on the one hand, they must guard against risks to economic growth, and on the other, they need to limit the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, economic performance was robust in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist, which will partly depend on the extent to which the rapid growth of the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressures on growth posed by the further advancement of structural reforms. Due to stabilizing economic conditions and subsiding risks, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has become increasingly solid since late 2016, growth in both advanced and emerging market economies accelerated synchronously in 2017. Among major advanced economies, the US saw a steady rise in investment and exports, driven by improving private sector optimism and a significant depreciation of the US dollar, while the euro area and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from stabilizing global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the short term, following the passage of tax reform in the US, investment and consumption are expected to be further boosted by corporate and personal income tax cuts. In view of the current cyclical economic upturn and the expansionary effects brought about by the US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP Growth Forecasts With strengthening growth momentum in the euro area and Japan, the market expected the divergence in global monetary policies to narrow; coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, this stimulated an increase in risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the US dollar. Although the Federal Reserve raised interest rates three times during the year and began advancing its balance sheet normalization, the US dollar index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite the broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained weak and below their central banks' targets, leading the market to expect, until recently, that global interest rates would remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global stock markets continued to trend higher in 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 Index repeatedly hitting new highs, pushing the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio up to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest level since the "dot-com bubble" in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core Inflation in Major Advanced Economies However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would lead to higher fiscal deficits and inflation have caused long-term US Treasury yields to climb continuously, raising doubts about the sustainability of increasingly high asset market valuations. As the US announced higher-than-expected average hourly earnings growth for January 2018, the market reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global stock markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 Index plunged by over 10% at one point from its peak on January 26, completely wiping out the significant gains made early in the year, and remained under pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged sharply, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) spiking to a two-year high of 37.3 at one point, marking the end of the persistently narrow trading range environment of the past two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, following the short-term stock market volatility, US inflation risks, upside risks to long-term US bond yields, and potential monetary policy tightening by other major central banks could all lead to a tightening of global monetary conditions, which in turn would cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, regarding US inflation risks, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions that are expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The main measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates, (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investments, and (3) a one-time "deemed repatriation" provision that helps reduce the incentive for US companies to park their overseas earnings abroad. Although it remains uncertain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy having now reached its output potential, the tax cuts could potentially push US output further beyond its potential, subsequently leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If the rise in inflationary pressures exceeds expectations, it may prompt the Federal Reserve to accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening. Currently, the path of the federal funds rate expected by financial markets is flatter than the projections released by the Federal Reserve. However, if inflation rebounds unexpectedly, the risk of a sudden recalibration of rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal Funds Rate Projections Second, given that the tax reform may exacerbate the fiscal deficit, the issuance of US Treasuries is expected to increase in the future. As the Federal Reserve continues to implement its balance sheet normalization program, which is expected to lead to an increase in the term premium, the increased issuance of US Treasuries under these circumstances could exacerbate the upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Furthermore, as market expectations for the passage of the US tax cut plan increased, US inflation expectations have continued to rise since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). Consequently, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen by over 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased Treasury supply pressures and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 5-Year, 5-Year Forward Inflation Expectation In addition, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain low for a prolonged period as widely expected. Although estimates of R* vary, it is generally believed to have fallen significantly since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, US R* may face upside risks in the future due to (1) a decline in the national savings rate resulting from expected increases in fiscal deficits, and (2) a potential rise in the investment rate driven by corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment for capital expenditures. A rise in R*, along with an expected increase in the term premium resulting from the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalization, could portend higher long-term interest rates, thereby creating headwinds for asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R* Estimated by the Laubach-Williams Model Third, strengthening growth momentum in the euro area and Japan has led to market expectations that their central banks may scale back monetary easing measures. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. In the euro area, member economies recorded broad-based cyclical expansions (Chart 2.7). As for Japan, the economic recovery also accelerated, with real GDP recording its eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan continued to signal the maintenance of accommodative monetary policies amid sluggish inflation, the brightening economic growth prospects in the euro area and Japan (and the persistently tightening labor market in Japan) have led some market participants to predict that they will further taper their quantitative easing programs in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real GDP of Selected Euro Area Member States Policy and event risks stemming from international politics and geopolitical tensions could also pose a threat to the nascent recovery in global economic growth and trade. The US government appears more inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, with recent examples being the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines in January 2018, and on steel and aluminum in early March, raising concerns over whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. Meanwhile, negotiations are currently underway between the UK and the rest of the EU regarding post-Brexit trade arrangements, a process fraught with multiple uncertainties. If these developments lead to increased trade frictions, they could hinder global trade flows and reduce global productive efficiency. Furthermore, any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions (such as military conflicts on the Korean Peninsula, political turmoil in the Middle East, and latent risks of terrorist attacks) could increase volatility in global financial markets. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, concluding the year with a robust performance. Real growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the primary driver of growth, while domestic demand also provided stable support (Chart 2.8). The accelerated recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China, and a rebound in global demand for tech products all propelled the region's exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: Domestic Demand and Exports Inflationary pressures have remained subdued so far. In the second half of 2017, headline inflation in East Asia moderated, influenced by lower food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, due to sluggish wage growth in several economies, core CPI inflation (excluding food and energy) remained at a relatively low level. Chart 2.9 East Asia: Headline and Core CPI Inflation* *Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a tolerance band of +/- 0.5%. Source: CEIC and respective central banks. The improving economy was accompanied by massive capital inflows, leading to a significant rise in financial asset prices in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10). The volume of capital flowing into regional markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching a new high since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose in tandem with the market. In fact, credit risk premiums in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, and benchmark stock indices across the region rose across the board. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

With robust domestic demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. The local economic outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, such as the normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, the stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiments, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, although domestic inflation pressures should remain moderate, certain upside risks still exist. The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. The seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, comparable to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow solidly and remained one of the major drivers of GDP growth. The solid growth in consumption was underpinned by favorable employment and income conditions, still-optimistic consumer sentiment, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, increased corporate capital expenditure led to a significant rebound in overall investment spending in the final quarter, following broadly stable performance in the preceding three quarters. On the external front, benefiting from the improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as the growth of imports outpaced that of exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports The sustained economic growth momentum led to an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment increased by about 0.7% to over 3.85 million, with the most notable increases seen in the construction, financing and business services, and public administration, social and personal services sectors. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labor productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from the improved global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue to grow, mainly driven by favorable labor market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage debt service burden on private consumption. As for domestic fixed capital formation, building and construction activities should grow steadily, benefiting from the increased housing supply and the continuous rollout of infrastructure projects. Although the improving economic environment will stimulate business capital expenditure, potential interest rate hikes may bring negative impacts. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3% to 4% for 2018, while growth forecasts by international organizations and private sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in previous sections, the economic performance of Mainland China under tightening financial conditions, and the trajectory of the local asset market. Domestic inflation pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, but month-on-month inflation momentum has shown signs of a slight pickup in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, comparable to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the annualized 3-month rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Within this, the prices of both tradables and services increased. The rebound in newly-let private residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labor cost pressures have remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 CCPI rental component and market rentals Chart 3.5 Unit labor cost and per capita salary As global inflation remains moderate and domestic cost increases are stable, Hong Kong's inflation pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2018, but the underlying inflation rate may gradually recover from the eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, due to the pass-through effect of the increase in newly-let private residential rentals, inflation pressures may increase somewhat in the second half of 2018. The market consensus forecasts a moderate headline inflation rate of 2.2% for 2018, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks still exist. On the external front, if global inflation or commodity prices record larger-than-expected increases, domestic inflation momentum could increase. On the domestic front, the labor market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, dropping below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero; if the labor market tightens significantly, it could pose additional upside pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate Following the low interest rates after the 2008 global financial crisis, the mortgage debt of Hong Kong households has increased. With the progression of US dollar interest rate normalization, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow US dollar interest rates upwards, and the household mortgage debt service burden will correspondingly increase in the future, thereby dragging on household consumption. Therefore, this Box examines the impact of an increased mortgage debt service burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage debt service burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt service payments (i.e., interest payments plus principal amortization) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage debt service burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, and the wealth and collateral effects induced by asset price changes mentioned in general economic theory, in the presence of a mortgage debt service burden, interest rate shocks will also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments, which in turn changes households' disposable income. This impact will magnify with an increase in the outstanding mortgage loan amount. Furthermore, the principal amortization amount will vary with changes in the outstanding mortgage loan amount, which will also affect private consumption by altering household disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption To measure the impact of the mortgage debt service burden on private consumption, we estimated the Outstanding Mortgage Debt Service Ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike current mortgage debt service burden indicators that only apply to newly-drawn mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of the entire household sector, which is more closely related to aggregate private consumption. We broadly followed the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements and measured the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed installment payments: where Dt is the outstanding residential mortgage loan amount of the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage debt service burden of the entire household sector, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt service burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the OMDSR estimates from 1985 to mid-2017, as well as the median mortgage payment and loan repayment to income ratio estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population census. In the early 2000s, both ratios exhibited a downward trend, which coincided with the decline in overall household mortgage borrowing following the burst of the property market bubble in 1997 and the sharp fall in mortgage interest rates during the same period. Despite the substantial increase in property prices after the global financial crisis, these two ratios remained stable, as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) adopted macroprudential measures on bank mortgage lending, which contained overall household mortgage leverage. In addition, the lengthening of the maturity of newly-drawn mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and the median mortgage payment and loan repayment to income ratio We also compared the OMDSR with the banks' debt servicing ratio (DSR), which is the actual debt servicing to income ratio of banks' new mortgage applicants. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than the banks' DSR, partly because the OMDSR covers not only newly-drawn mortgages but also existing mortgages. Since existing mortgages were originated when property prices were lower, their payments are correspondingly lower than those of newly-drawn mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage debt service burden indicator covering both existing and newly-drawn mortgages (i.e., the OMDSR) will be lower than the debt service burden indicator for newly-drawn mortgages (i.e., the banks' DSR). Furthermore, the higher banks' DSR is also due to banks complying with the HKMA's prudential supervisory requirements by taking into account non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the DSR. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and the banks' DSR remained stable, mainly due to the HKMA's implementation of prudential supervision on mortgage lending, which set a cap on the banks' DSR, and this measure also helped to stabilize the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks' DSR for newly-drawn mortgages Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt service burden indicators, but the OMDSR has stronger timeliness and can reflect the burden of overall outstanding mortgage debt, rather than just the burden of newly-drawn mortgage debt. Therefore, we believe that using the OMDSR can assess the impact of the mortgage debt service burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage debt service burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimated an error-correction model following the methodologies of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-term relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term in the short-term equation. Based on existing theories and empirical evidence, we used real income (proxied by median household income, deflated by the CCPI), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index respectively, deflated by the CCPI), and the OMDSR as the long-term determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, although the pace of growth moderated compared with the first half. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy continues its normalization, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. If global financial market sentiment shifts abruptly, the volatility of fund flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate briefly strengthened and hovered around the 7.80 level between September and November 2017. This was mainly driven by tighter liquidity conditions resulting from increased funding demand for initial public offering (IPO) activities and banks' prudent liquidity management towards the month-end and year-end, which in turn led to a slowdown in interest rate arbitrage activities and an increase in the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. As the tight Hong Kong dollar liquidity conditions eased and commercial demand for the US dollar increased towards the year-end, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (especially equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar weakened, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Fund Flow Indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated within a narrow range in the second half of 2017, but has recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly in line with the movements of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to track the movements of the nominal effective exchange rate index closely. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest Balance of Payments statistics showed that portfolio investment in equities by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting the improved economic outlook in the region and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Portfolio investment in debt securities by non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting the outflows of debt investment by residents. A survey on global mutual funds also indicated that, driven by optimistic market sentiment towards the economic outlook and corporate earnings, both equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that despite the correction in global financial markets, equity investments continued to record inflows, while bond investments recorded mild fund outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market Survey on Equity and Bond Related Fund Flows Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy normalization process continues, the negative interest rate spread between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may lead to an increase in arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking of the Hong Kong dollar being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. At the same time, given the uncertainties surrounding the pace of US monetary policy normalization and the rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, the volatility of Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully ensure the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite the interest rate hikes and ongoing balance sheet reduction by the US Federal Reserve, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base rose further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by the increase in Certificates of Indebtedness issued to back the issuance of banknotes (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the Aggregate Balance and the total amount of outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly unchanged at around HK$1,226.8 billion in the second half of the year. Within this total, the Aggregate Balance shrank, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totaling HK$80 billion) to meet banks' strong demand for liquidity management. Entering 2018, the Monetary Base remained stable despite the correction in the stock market. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, but at a slower pace. The growth of the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) decelerated from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose slightly by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Among them, demand deposits grew at a faster pace in the second half, partly due to the buoyant asset markets and increased investment demand. An analysis of the counterpart assets shows that the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 was supported by the strong growth of Hong Kong dollar loans on the one hand (Chart 4.6), but dragged down by the net outflow of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and the contraction in banks' net foreign currency assets on the other. Chart 4.6 Hong Kong dollar M3 and Changes in its Counterpart Assets On the other hand, the growth of foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits declined from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits rebounded significantly by 8.4% in the second half after declining continuously for over two years. This was mainly driven by the recent rebound in renminbi deposits. Due to the slower growth of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits, total deposits with authorized institutions increased modestly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with a growth of 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to that in 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit Growth Between September and December 2017, increased funding demand for IPO activities and banks' prudent liquidity management towards the month-end and year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). The overnight and 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively relative to six months ago, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% respectively in December (on a monthly average basis). The negative interest rate spreads between the 1-month to 3-month HIBORs and their US dollar counterparts also narrowed accordingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Interest Rates Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards but flattened, broadly tracking the movements of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds recorded a smaller increase of 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate and Average Interest Rate for New Mortgage Loans Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As the year-end funding demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates eased in early January. Thereafter, despite the corrections in global and local stock markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained broadly stable. The overnight and 3-month HIBORs closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks' lending rates rose along with the spike in Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates, banks' funding costs generally remained low due to the still-large deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage loan business, the average interest rate for new mortgage loans of banks gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the upward trend of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the Composite Interest Rate, a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, briefly rose in October due to increased funding demand for IPO activities, but remained soft for most of the second half, closing at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy continues its normalization, coupled with the possible initiation of interest rate normalization by other major economies, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase the volatility of fund flows. However, the large Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base can serve as a buffer, helping to mitigate excessively rapid increases in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks' prudent liquidity management and the availability of discounting through the Discount Window also help to contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate reached 10.2% in the first half, but moderated to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). The growth of both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed in the second half of 2017. Analyzed by currency, supported by the favorable local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans only edged up by 0.1%. Among them, the growth of US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to rising US dollar funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total loans recorded a strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan Growth The growth of loans for use in Hong Kong (including trade finance) declined from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major economic sectors (Chart 4.11). The growth of loans for building, construction, property development and investment slowed in the second half, partly because the authorities required banks to strengthen credit risk management for loans to property developers starting from June 2017. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade finance and the transport sector only recorded relatively mild increases, while loans for the wholesale and retail trade sector recorded a decline. Conversely, loan growth for financial concerns remained strong, reflecting to some extent the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Domestic Loan Growth by Selected Sectors Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with an increase of 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loan growth (including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes) accelerated further, reaching 12.4% in the second half. The strong personal loan growth was mainly driven by borrowing from private banking and wealth management clients secured by financial assets. The growth of these loans was broadly in line with the continuous growth of client assets managed by banks. The risks associated with such secured loans are within a manageable range. In addition, the HKMA issued guidelines on personal loan risk management to banks in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting caps on loan tenors and borrowers' debt-servicing ratios. On the other hand, although residential property transaction volume increased, the loan-to-value ratios for newly approved mortgages declined, and the growth of residential mortgage loans edged down slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the ratio of household debt to gross domestic product rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Mainly benefiting from the growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared to the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. After experiencing strong growth in the first half of 2017, credit growth slowed in the second half of the year, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a significant increase in Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates (HIBOR), the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks remained at a low level due to low retail deposit rates. However, banks should be vigilant against the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows under the normalization of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. As corporate leverage continues to rise and personal debt burdens also remain high, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality if interest rates rise more than expected. To enhance banks' resilience against systemic risks, Hong Kong's countercyclical capital buffer ratio will be increased to 2.5% effective from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 13.6% year-on-year. This mainly benefited from a substantial increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment charges, which were sufficient to offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets of retail banks edged down to 1.15% in the second half of 2017 from 1.17% in the first half. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 was still higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For the full year of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose to 1.16% from 1.09% in 2016. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks further widened to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Observational evidence shows that the improvement in the net interest margin is consistent with the rise in the average spread of Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average spread of Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans Since September 2017, HIBOR has risen across the board, mainly driven by liquidity demand related to initial public offerings and banks' funding needs towards the year-end, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. Among them, the 3-month HIBOR recorded a post-financial crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up 53 basis points from the end of June, but remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Entering 2018, as banks' year-end liquidity demand eased, HIBOR appeared to have stabilized. Despite the recent rise in HIBOR, the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks remained stable. This was mainly due to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Under these circumstances, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, remained at a low level of around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up recently to 0.38% at the end of December (green line in Chart 5.4). A similar situation was observed in the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, banks' average Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs in the non-deposit market rose by 35 basis points, while the average deposit funding cost edged up by 12 basis points. Overall, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturity of licensed banks The magnitude of the increase in HIBOR exceeded that of the overall funding costs of the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve the interest spread of banks' HIBOR-priced assets. However, this improvement may be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market data shows that some banks have reduced the spread between their mortgage rates and the benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given the expectation of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. Given the intense competition in the loan market, if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this could put pressure on banks' net interest margins. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above the international minimum standard, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector remains well-capitalized. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at the end of June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio 54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. 55 Chart 5.6 Capitalization of locally incorporated authorized institutions The HKMA recently published a consultation paper to consult on the rules for setting loss-absorbing capacity requirements for authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorized institutions helps reduce the likelihood of a financial crisis and thereby benefits society, it will inevitably incur costs. Feature 5 conducts a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of the loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment shows that implementing the loss-absorbing capacity requirements will bring net benefits to the Hong Kong economy. Measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the 80% statutory minimum requirement applicable for 2017. Although the average liquidity maintenance ratio of category 2 institutions edged down from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the 25% statutory minimum requirement. The abundant liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is able to withstand liquidity shocks caused by potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, as one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce banks' medium- to long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable funding sources to finance their business activities. Specifically, category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of not less than 100% at all times. 57 Customer deposits remained the primary funding source for authorized institutions, reflecting that the banking system maintained a stable funding structure. At the end of December 2017, the proportion of customer deposits to the total liabilities of all authorized institutions was broadly the same as six months ago, remaining at 56.2% (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 77.1% at the end of June 2017 to 82.7% at the end of December (Chart 5.9), reflecting that the growth rate of Hong Kong dollar loans and advances outpaced that of deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as the growth rate of foreign currency deposits outpaced that of loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 65.5% at the end of June 2017 to 63.1% at the end of December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies rose to 73.0% from 71.4% six months ago. Banks should assess the impact of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio on their liquidity management. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a low level. We estimate that under a hypothetical shock of a 200-basis-point parallel upward shift in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, given the expectation that the US Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates and proceed with balance sheet normalization, banks should assess the impact of this situation on their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.10 Impact of interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks In the second half of 2017, under a mild but still benign economic environment, the growth rate of total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed to 5.3% from the strong growth of 10.2% recorded in the first half. After experiencing two years of slowing growth, total loans grew solidly by 16.1% for the full year of 2017. The asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions declined to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, compared to 0.84% and 0.61% respectively at the end of June. For retail banks, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth of loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks' asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and therefore banks should closely monitor their credit risks.
