Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and plays an important role in global supply chains, when the epidemic disrupts its production activities and drags down its economic growth, it will cause significant spillover effects and potentially affect the entire world (Chart 2.3). Since late February, the surge in coronavirus infection cases outside Mainland China may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose a risk of directly dragging down local economic activities. 5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread. Chart 2.3 Exports of Goods and Services to Mainland China by Selected Major Advanced Economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP). To cope with the potential severe economic shocks caused by the epidemic, some central banks (including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, and some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face immense selling pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which in turn may exacerbate the downward pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index. In addition to the development of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. Particularly regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have decreased following the phase one trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations may be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain to be resolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to be smooth, thereby prolonging post-Brexit uncertainties. In addition, the sharp drop in oil prices since March will exert pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, due to sluggish global demand, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019. East Asia's exports to major destinations such as the US, European economies, and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downcycle of technology products in the region is bottoming out, including reports from large regional electronics companies that their earnings improved at the end of 2019 6, it remains to be seen whether there will be a substantial rebound in the region's technology product exports. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise Exports to Major Destinations. Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also plagued investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation in most East Asian economies declining in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which may affect the region's potential economic growth in the long run. To support economic growth in a mild inflation environment, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea lowered their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting rates in the first half of the year, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross Fixed Capital Formation. The coronavirus outbreak has led to concerns that regional economies may face further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As multiple economies in the region have imposed travel restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry has borne the brunt, with economies more reliant on Mainland Chinese tourists and tourism service exports being particularly affected by this epidemic (Chart 2.7). The continuation and intensification of the epidemic will also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Tourists. In the short term, this epidemic will continue to affect economic activities and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these impacts may be short-lived, but the actual situation will depend on the severity and spread of the epidemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although the market expects corporate earnings to deteriorate in the short term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions have encouraged search-for-yield activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. Therefore, regional stock markets are more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected Earnings of Constituent Stocks in Benchmark Equity Indices. Second, the weakness in corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private entities in the region to service their debts. Although the decline in local interest rates can provide breathing space for indebted companies and households, it may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as discussed in Box 1, when more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, the risk of debt overhang for private entities may also intensify, although this impact may be limited to enterprises with sounder financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowings. Third, regarding external factors, East Asian economies may also face increased risks in the face of US trade policies with increasingly tough protectionist barriers. Despite recent progress on the phase one trade agreement between China and the US, Sino-US trade tensions persist as fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain. As evidenced by the growing trade surpluses of multiple regional economies with the US (Chart 2.9), multinational companies may continue to seek more supply channels outside the China-centric supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the US had increased to approximately USD 167 billion. If their trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, the relevant Asian economies could become the next targets of the trade war; for example, the US government imposed hefty tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In view of this, despite the Sino-US trade truce, the region's trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise Trade Surpluses with the US. Over the past decade, the deepening integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds. 8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds) but also actively managed funds that reference investment indices. 9 By bringing in overseas investors that the relevant economies would otherwise be unable to attract or reach, these funds help promote the financial market development of emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, contributing to the long-term growth and stability of the markets. However, is there really a free lunch? Regarding passive bond funds, there are market concerns that investments by such funds may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, thereby leading to high corporate leverage levels. 10 Furthermore, it has been suggested that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has exacerbated the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies—which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors—even more vulnerable. 11 This box assesses the impact of index-driven investments on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to the constituent bonds of a benchmark index according to their weights in the index. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may leave the issuers of index constituent bonds lacking the incentive to act in the interests of fund investors. 13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behavior may fuel excessive borrowing, bringing significant credit and debt-servicing risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, whose leverage ratio has risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies. Using the weights of enterprises from various emerging market economies in a mainstream index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as an estimate of their bonds' exposure to passive bond fund investments, 14 we find that an increase in such investments will push up the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratio of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond markets in emerging market economies, the expanded long-term bond investor base brought about by passive bond funds is also conducive to the development of enterprises in emerging market economies. We also find that the above effect is only significant for emerging market enterprises with sounder fundamentals (especially those with stronger debt-servicing capacity and a lower leverage ratio) (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged enterprises or those with poorer debt-servicing capacity seem, conversely, not to fall further into the debt trap due to investments by passive bond funds. In conclusion, the above study shows that the growth of passive bond fund investments may not significantly increase the debt-servicing risks of the corporate sectors in emerging market economies.

Due to weakening private consumption, reduced investment expenditure, and poor export performance, the Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. It is expected that the economic performance in 2020 will face significant challenges, and the recent coronavirus epidemic has also brought substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, such as slowing global economic growth, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and the development of local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate will likely climb further in 2020. Local inflation pressures are expected to ease somewhat, although the outlook faces potential upside and downside risks. The Hong Kong economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the whole year, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, marking the first annual contraction recorded since the 2009 global financial crisis. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components. On a quarter-to-quarter basis, economic activities slowed down significantly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, thereby weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer sentiment, so private consumption contracted significantly starting from the third quarter. 33 Due to increased economic uncertainties and worsening business sentiment, overall investment expenditure remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter. 34 Externally, with the escalation of China-US trade frictions, weakening global economic growth, and a sharp plunge in visitor arrivals, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish (Chart 3.2). 35 Under the impact of a sharp contraction in services exports, net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter, but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports. Given the immense headwinds facing the economy, the Government rolled out multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to ease the financial burden on the public, safeguard jobs, and support enterprises, particularly supporting small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) and severely hit sectors such as retail, food services, transport, and tourism. 36 To allow banks more room to step up support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on October 14 a reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, including small and medium-sized enterprise (SME). It is expected that Hong Kong's economic performance in 2020 will face significant challenges, and the epidemic has recently brought substantial downside risks as well. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruptions caused by the social incidents, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020-21 Budget can provide relief to households and enterprises (especially small and medium-sized enterprise (SME)), including the disbursement of a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and the provision of a concessionary low-interest loan with a 100% Government guarantee for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme (SFGS). 37 The HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, which will allow banks more room to step up support for the local economy, especially for sectors and individuals facing greater pressure in the short term due to the impact of the epidemic. Analyzed by GDP components, private consumption and investment will likely remain weak due to fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the phase one China-US trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to drag down Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to supply chain disruptions in the region and a slowdown in cross-boundary economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by the numerous uncertainties and risks mentioned in the preceding chapters. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Among them, the unemployment rate for the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors surged to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe blow dealt by the social incidents. 39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly seen in the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real payroll also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labor market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is highly likely to climb further. Feature Article 3 will explore the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labor market in greater detail. Chart 3.3 Labor market conditions. Local inflation pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activities weakened, inflation momentum also gradually slowed down. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (Composite CPI) grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, and the increase moderated slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The annualized three-month rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, also eased from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflation momentum was due to reduced price pressures on various CPI components. Regarding tradable goods, basic food inflation remained visible due to rising fresh pork prices, but price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear, as well as durable goods, remained mild. Regarding services, with the slower growth in newly let private housing rentals earlier, the increase in the rental component of the CPI also showed a downward trend (Chart 3.5). Labor cost pressures rose slightly but remained at a mild level in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation. Chart 3.5 Composite CPI rental component and market rentals. Chart 3.6 Unit labor cost. It is expected that local inflation pressures will ease somewhat in the near term. Domestically, the weak economic conditions and the widened negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private housing rentals continue to moderate, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. Externally, imported inflation is expected to remain mild due to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate in 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5% and the headline inflation rate at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economic deterioration is more severe than expected (for example, due to the continuation of the coronavirus epidemic), inflation could be further suppressed. On the other hand, if the disruption to the fresh pork supply becomes more severe, it will bring upside pressure to inflation. Despite the visible slowdown in the Hong Kong economy, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8-2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate climbed more visibly to 3.3% at the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus epidemic, the labor market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this feature article analyzes the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labor market, including exploring why the overall labor market was broadly resilient (with the unemployment rate remaining virtually unchanged) in the first three quarters of 2019, and what implications this has for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is noteworthy that, partly because adjusting labor demand entails costs, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate often lags behind the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activities deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real GDP growth rate and unemployment rate. On the labor demand front, although the tense China-US trade situation and local social incidents dealt a heavy blow to employment in the trade and retail and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors were still able to support the overall labor market. Specifically, employment in the financing, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the impact of the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained robust, and financial activities in terms of fintech development and initial public offerings were also very active. These factors may have helped support the employment market in the financing and business services sectors. In addition, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, which include education, healthcare, and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to economic cycles. Correlation coefficient analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the response of the public administration, social and personal services sectors to economic cycles is more neutral. In other words, even if the economy slows down, employment in these sectors may not be subject to significant cyclical impacts. Chart B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019. On the labor supply front, the labor force participation rate 40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors affecting the changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, with the significant economic contraction in the second half of the year, the decrease in employment exerted upside pressure on the unemployment rate. Taken together, although employment decreased during the economic recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped mitigate the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors leading to changes in the unemployment rate. Some changes in the structure of the labor market are also worth noting. In particular, the increased proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the proportions of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment have declined to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, but the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second largest group in the total employed population (about 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, companies may be able to retain or hire more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to about 44 hours currently, partly reflecting that there are more part-time workers in the employed population today.

The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate has strengthened since October, with its upward momentum further increasing in December, keeping the HKD exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months. The strong demand for the HKD was partly driven by equity-related demand, and partly due to the unwinding of HKD short positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards the end of the year. Overall, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although market sentiment triggered by the coronavirus epidemic under an uncertain external environment may lead to increased volatility in fund flows, Hong Kong has massive foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, making it capable of withstanding the pressure of capital outflows without affecting the city's financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related HKD demand (including initial public offerings (IPOs)), the HKD exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the HKD further strengthened. From mid-December to February, the HKD exchange rate remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone. The strengthening of the HKD exchange rate was partly due to buoyant IPO activities, and partly due to the unwinding of HKD short positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards the end of the year. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the HKD exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, HKD trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 HKD Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes The nominal effective exchange rate index (NEERI) of the HKD broadly tracked the movements of the US dollar (USD) and edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and thus had a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index (REERI) of the HKD, the movement of the HKD REERI broadly followed that of the NEERI. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates When measuring Hong Kong's fund flows, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) HKD fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flow. HKD fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows, which helps assess monetary stability, especially under the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). On the other hand, cross-border fund flow focuses on the geographical movement of funds through the Hong Kong banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. The two fund flow concepts require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring HKD fund flows, one needs to focus on the HKD exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert their HKD assets into foreign currency assets in large amounts, the demand for the HKD will naturally decline, leading to a weaker HKD exchange rate. Under the LERS, if the HKD exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA will stand ready to buy HKD at the request of banks, and the Aggregate Balance will subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, and the HKD exchange rate has been on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months; therefore, no significant fund outflows from the HKD were observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, total bank deposits in Hong Kong serve as a useful indicator. When there are massive capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decrease. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there were no noticeable cross-border fund outflows. The Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus epidemic on the local monetary environment remains limited. However, we need to closely monitor the risks brought about by the outbreak of the coronavirus epidemic. Hong Kong possesses massive foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to cope with capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and the local economic slowdown, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The HKD Monetary Base remained large, rising by 4.0% since the end of June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, the broad HKD money supply indicators remained broadly stable. The broad HKD money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and subsequently edged up by 0.2% during the seven-month period since the end of June 2019. An analysis of counterpart assets shows that the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 since the end of June mainly reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets and a rise in the Monetary Base (driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation) (Chart 4.5). During the seven-month period since the end of June, Hong Kong dollar deposits (a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3) remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting the rise in HKD deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and Counterpart Assets During the seven-month period since the end of June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by USD deposits, which increased by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% over the same period, among which renminbi (RMB) deposits recorded a slight decline in HKD terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since the end of June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may be subject to volatility driven by various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), these statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with Authorized Institutions by Currency Chart 4.7 Total Broad Money Supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term HKD Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) experienced volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, as IPO activities in the Hong Kong stock market became active, the overnight HIBOR occasionally exhibited larger fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term HIBORs generally increased. Subscriptions for large-scale IPOs exert significant pressure on the overnight HIBOR. Empirical analysis in Box 4 shows that market attention to future IPO activities also affects the 3-month HIBOR. This situation occurs if market participants anticipate the future subscription closing dates of large-scale IPOs and prepare medium-term funds in advance for early deployment. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD Interbank Offered Rates As for the HKD yield curve, it shifted downwards tracking the USD yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate and Average Interest Rate for New Mortgage Loans At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This increase mainly reflected that banks continued to raise promotional deposit rates to attract deposit funds, leading to a rise in the weighted HKD deposit rate. At the end of October 2019, following the downward adjustment of the target range for the US federal funds rate, a number of retail banks lowered their best lending rates (BLRs) by 12.5 basis points. Therefore, the BLRs of retail banks currently range from 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding mortgage loans, for HIBOR-based mortgage loans, major banks raised the interest rate caps determined by the BLRs, causing the average interest rate for new mortgage loans to rise to around 2.63% in October. 45 With the BLRs in the market being lowered since November, the average mortgage loan rate subsequently decreased slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus epidemic to US economic activities, and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy goals, the Federal Reserve lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although HIBORs track USD interest rates in the long run, short-term HIBORs may be influenced by local factors that could affect HKD demand, such as IPO activities in Hong Kong. As the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has decreased since April 2018, the sensitivity of HIBORs to changes in the supply and demand of HKD funds may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet the demand for interbank payment and settlement. In fact, the Hong Kong interbank market has been operating in an orderly manner. In the event of short-term liquidity tightness, banks can utilize the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA for banks. Given the potential escalation of the US-China trade conflict, the offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore RMB against the USD falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Entering October, as the market anticipated the resumption of US-China trade talks, the depreciation trend of the RMB reversed. The offshore and onshore RMB strengthened in the fourth quarter and, following the signing of the phase one trade agreement between the US and China, briefly broke through the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020. However, since the end of January, due to the outbreak of the coronavirus epidemic, the offshore and onshore RMB have once again faced depreciation pressure. The offshore RMB traded at a discount to the onshore RMB for most of the time between May and August, but generally traded at a premium in the latter part of 2019. The discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, but the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates Despite the volatility in the RMB exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore RMB interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the 3-month offshore RMB HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore RMB HIBOR experienced brief volatility in late August and late November due to the MSCI A-share rebalancing, and in late January 2020 approaching the Lunar New Year holidays.

Due to increasing uncertainties in the global and domestic economic environments, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained at a healthy level by historical standards. Although total loan growth slowed in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the period under review. As a result, the average loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions both increased. However, given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system stood at a stable level and deposits remained broadly stable, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continuous rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks 59 fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. As a result, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% recorded in the same period of 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), their net interest income continued to record moderate growth during the period under review. However, both loan impairment charges and operating expenses of retail banks increased, leading to a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite the US federal funds target rate being cut three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market has not yet seen significant downward pressure. Conversely, driven by various local factors (including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand due to large-scale initial public offerings, and tighter interbank market liquidity conditions), short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, longer-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained broadly stable during the period under review, with the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to the level six months ago (blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, there was limited room for retail banks to follow suit in cutting interest rates after the US lowered its policy rate. 60 On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the period under review, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funding. 61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) rose gradually from 0.95% six months ago to 1.09% at the end of 2019, although it remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, given that the decline in US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding costs, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the period under review, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs and the relatively high level of Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates, providing support to banking sector profitability over the same period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local framework for interest rate risk in the banking book have been submitting returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding costs and maturities have been calculated as a weighted average based on the relevant figures of these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be directly compared with those of previous months. Looking ahead, multiple downside risk factors in the external and domestic environments will continue to cloud the profitability outlook of banks. Relevant factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of US-China trade relations, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors may dampen the already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce the demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist, which may exert pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, the local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to hit business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even further intensifies in the future, it may lead to a deterioration in the credit demand outlook and banks' asset quality. Regarding overall market development, following the granting of eight virtual bank licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector has begun to launch virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by launching more convenient products and offering more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this may exert upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. Although the short-term impact may remain mild as the current business scale of virtual banks is still limited, the long-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks will accelerate the adoption of fintech to maintain their competitiveness. The results of Feature 5 show that the degree of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically correlated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability levels. The capitalization of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above minimum international standards. As of the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated authorized institutions In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, there is also the non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement under Basel III to restrict excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio 65 requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the period under review. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions also rose moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio 66, as one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, indicates that the funding positions of authorized institutions are stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of Category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of Category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the applicable statutory minimum requirement of 75% for 2019. The ample liquidity and robust funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting that the banking system maintained a stable funding structure. At the end of 2019, the proportion of customer deposits to total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained largely unchanged, edging down slightly to 56.3% from 56.4% six months ago (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions The average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.10), as the level of Hong Kong dollar loans and advances remained broadly stable while deposits fell slightly during the period under review. 67 Meanwhile, as the growth of foreign currency loans outpaced that of deposits, the average foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio also rose from 58.9% to 60.4% over the same period. Overall, the average loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies of all authorized institutions rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the same year. Given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has remained stable since April 2019 and deposits have remained broadly stable, there were no obvious signs of significant fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system during the period under review. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2019. We estimate that under an assumed shock of a 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of US-China trade tensions, a global economic slowdown, and ongoing local social incidents, bank credit growth slowed in the second half of 2019 after a moderate rebound in the first half. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth (measured by the change in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions) grew moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was due to the moderating growth trends in both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans for use outside Hong Kong during the period under review. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, lower than the increases of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, total loan growth for the full year of 2019 still rose moderately to 6.7%, higher than the 4.4% recorded for the full year of 2018.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines has brought hope for reopening the economy, boosting the global growth outlook. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing policies, financial markets have repeatedly hit new highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery is expected to be uneven across economies. In the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high debt levels, and the long-lasting economic scarring caused by the pandemic will be challenges facing policymakers in the future. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking against the US dollar, driven mainly by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, and there were no signs of significant capital outflows from the local banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activity and reduced credit demand caused by the recurring pandemic, total loans in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, although a slight increase was still recorded for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but global growth slowed again as COVID-19 infection numbers resurged from the fourth quarter onwards. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development in late 2020, the market expects the pandemic to eventually end, which is conducive to the global economy returning to normal and accelerating growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing policies, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies may lead to higher-than-expected inflation, which in turn may prompt central banks to taper monetary easing earlier than expected, ending financial markets' expectations of a "lower for longer" monetary policy. Over the longer term, policymakers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the numerous economic legacies triggered by the pandemic, including high global debt and long-lasting economic scarring. In the East Asian region, supported by a rebound in export demand, gross domestic product (GDP) growth improved in the second half of 2020. Amid increased risk appetite, portfolio capital inflows to the region rebounded, and search-for-yield activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, the East Asian region still faces persistent uncertainties brought about by the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, variables in vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, coupled with the weakening fiscal positions of governments in the region, may dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of capital flows. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook still depends largely on the development of the pandemic and changes in Sino-US tensions. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi recorded several months of depreciation in early 2020, but subsequently strengthened for the remainder of the year amid an accelerated economic recovery, a weaker US dollar, and strong capital inflows into the Mainland bond market. Detailed studies show that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamental factors rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate fluctuations (for details, please refer to Feature 1). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in domestic demand and a further expansion in goods exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to rebound in the third quarter, ending the previous five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and also the first time in history that it recorded two consecutive years of decline, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by sector show that the contraction in consumption- and tourism-related sectors under the pandemic was worse than that of the overall economy. To cope with the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two more rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to help sectors and citizens affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021-22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of a 100% guaranteed personal concessionary loan for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced in March 2021 the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, and announced the extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines are expected to bring economic activities back to normal, and the local economy is expected to resume positive growth in 2021 (as a whole), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties such as the development of the pandemic and the progress and efficacy of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, which can provide support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their mass vaccination programmes. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% in 2021, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate climbed further, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, and the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. To cope with the continuously deteriorating labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain employees. Following the end of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support sectors hard hit by the pandemic. In the short term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Feature 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell significantly to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. The annualized 3-month rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, has also remained at a low level despite slight fluctuations in recent months. As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, local inflationary pressures are likely to remain mild in the near term; in particular, local inflation will continue to be contained by the slower growth in newly signed private residential rentals earlier. Market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate for 2021 to be at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the Government forecasts the underlying and headline inflation rates for 2021 to be 1.0% and 1.6% respectively. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking against the US dollar, driven mainly by equity-related funding demand, including from robust IPO fundraising activities and southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar strong. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with HK$263.3 billion of funds flowing into the Hong Kong dollar. The strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with a cumulative inflow of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Analyzed from a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from the local banking system. Although uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing Sino-US tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore well-equipped to withstand capital flow volatility. With the Aggregate Balance increasing as a result of the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates (HIBORs) generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. Due to the lower funding costs, the average lending rate for newly approved mortgages also dropped from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Following the strengthening of the onshore (CNY) exchange rate, the offshore renminbi (CNH) has appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with the outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB 826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi business, renminbi bank loans in Hong Kong decreased, while renminbi trade settlement grew, and the average daily turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system remained at a high level of RMB 1,191.5 billion for the whole of 2020. Hong Kong possesses highly efficient financial infrastructure, providing investors with numerous cross-border fund flow channels connecting to the Mainland. With the continued opening up of the Mainland's capital account, increasing demand for renminbi assets from international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by the rally in global stock markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors through the Stock Connect, the local stock market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. The rally in global stock markets was driven by factors including unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; market optimism over positive progress in vaccine development, which was seen as potentially helping to accelerate the recovery of economic activities; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recouped its losses following the sharp fall in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period, and briefly breached the 31,000 mark in mid-February 2021, hitting a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following significant net capital outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence recovered rapidly as governments worldwide rolled out unprecedented economic stimulus measures, leading to a rebound in bond fund inflows into the local market. Although bond yields rebounded mildly during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, continued to hover near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, the market expects the COVID-19 pandemic to eventually come to an end, enabling the global economy to accelerate its growth going forward. Coupled with the expectation of a "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors were not deterred by the resurgence of the pandemic in late 2020, and financial markets reached new highs in early 2021. However, the high expectations of the financial markets are somewhat disconnected from the still-challenging macroeconomic environment. Should the strength of the economic recovery fall short of expectations, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than expected (for example, due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices may experience volatility. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the dilemma of when to withdraw policy support and must address the many legacy issues left by the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-lasting economic scarring. The lingering uncertainties of the pandemic continue to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in the East Asian region, and the less developed emerging market economies in the region may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programmes could reverse the current optimism, destabilising capital inflows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, with consumption activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains highly uncertain, depending largely on the development of the pandemic and changes in Sino-US tensions. Therefore, the government announced that it would maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by economic reopenings, major economies mostly recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, COVID-19 infection numbers have climbed again, prompting governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, which once again weakened the global growth momentum. In late 2020, more transmissible variant viruses emerged and subsequently spread worldwide, making the situation even more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use in late 2020, the market expects the pandemic to eventually end, and the global economy to return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery comes from sustained policy stimulus measures, including the commitment by major central banks to a "lower for longer" monetary policy amid weak inflation, as well as continued fiscal easing measures in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. As a result, the International Monetary Fund revised its 2021 global GDP growth forecast upwards to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 forecast (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts made by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, and share prices of cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery rose, driving global share prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic situation remains challenging; the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets as they face multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control depends on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although there are global mechanisms (such as COVAX) to promote a more equitable distribution of vaccines, the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe due to limited vaccine supplies. If pandemic control is less than ideal, various regions may need to extend social distancing and other restrictive measures, thereby dampening the global recovery outlook. Chart 2.3 Share of the population having received at least one vaccine dose in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the rebound in financial markets is built on sustained monetary and fiscal policy support, especially the "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures may be withdrawn at a faster-than-expected pace. For example, under the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong money and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing policies, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already risen (Chart 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back their monetary easing policies, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4 US and Euro area 5-year/5-year forward inflation swap rates Third, there is significant uncertainty in future Sino-US relations. The wave of Sino-US "decoupling", particularly in the financial and technological sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly tough stance of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the US towards Mainland China, this trend may not necessarily reverse under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation in Sino-US tensions could trigger financial market turbulence in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to face the dilemma of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. Although a premature withdrawal of such measures could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect", over the longer term these measures are costly, including imposing fiscal burdens and delaying necessary post-pandemic resource reallocation, such as allowing "zombie firms" with unviable business models to survive with continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many legacy issues left by the pandemic. First, due to declining corporate revenues and surging government expenditures, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 (Chart 2.5). Although the problems brought about by the surge in debt may not be imminent given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, the continuous accumulation of debt in the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt-to-GDP ratio Another legacy issue involves the long-term economic losses or lasting scarring that the pandemic may cause. For instance, elevated uncertainty may lead businesses to reduce investment, while workers suffering from long-term unemployment may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a massive waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after a sharp plunge in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The momentum of economic recovery mainly came from a rebound in exports, with export demand for electronics and technological equipment being the most robust. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service sectors (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face contact with customers) continued to struggle. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite the lingering uncertainties surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have resumed flowing in. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted more bond inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced economy bonds (Chart 2.7). With signs of economic recovery and the rollout of vaccine production plans, equity inflows to the East Asian region also accelerated in the last quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated accordingly due to portfolio inflows, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index to rebound by about 10% from its lowest point in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment flows The East Asian region continues to face lingering uncertainties from the pandemic. First, although the rollout of vaccines brings hope to the region's hard-hit service sectors and economies, global competition for early batches of vaccines has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacities. Therefore, less developed economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, as investor optimism is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccinations falls significantly short of expectations, the current capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. A sudden drop in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turbulence. With the successful containment of COVID-19 and the gradual recovery of consumption, the Mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical equipment and high-tech products), exports also maintained growth (Chart 2.8). Looking at 2020 as a whole, despite the unprecedented shock to the economy from the COVID-19 pandemic, the Mainland's GDP still recorded a growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contributions of demand components to GDP growth Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economic recovery can be sustained will still depend to a certain extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the Mainland have normalised, the service sector remains partially disrupted as new outbreaks have re-emerged in several northern provinces. Regarding the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to the outbreak of new waves of the pandemic in most developed economies. In addition, Sino-US tensions may not ease in the short term, but the previously signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the concluded Comprehensive Agreement on Investment between China and the EU will help China further integrate with other economies, which may partially offset the adverse impact of Sino-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Considering that the economic outlook remains highly uncertain, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not undergo major changes in 2021 to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. Furthermore, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at over 6%. Over the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan sets technological self-reliance and the "dual circulation" strategy as priority development directions, with a view to bringing per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The outbreak of COVID-19 appears to have had a limited impact on the repayment ability of bond-issuing enterprises, and the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remained at a relatively low level in the second half of 2020. However, due to a sharp rise in bond defaults by state-owned enterprises, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 (Chart 2.9). Although the rise in state-owned enterprise defaults mainly reflects the central government's determination to break the "implicit guarantee" for state-owned enterprises to promote more rational market risk pricing, the limited fiscal space of some local governments may also be a contributing factor, especially for local governments in less developed regions. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Scale and ratio of onshore bond defaults In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Although the sustained economic recovery and the gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to the rise in financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default events occurred in the last quarter of 2020, causing credit spreads to widen significantly as a result (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields In the property market, Mainland housing prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in tier-1 cities. By contrast, the pace of housing price increases in lower-tier cities was much slower (Chart 2.11). As for the housing oversupply problem that had plagued tier-3 cities in previous years, it was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because tier-3 cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in tier-3 cities remained at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 alongside a revival in domestic demand and a further expansion in goods exports. With the hope that COVID-19 vaccinations will lead to a normalization of economic activities, the local economy is expected to resume growth in 2021, following the most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, such as the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. Therefore, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while domestic inflationary pressures will stay mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activities remained well below their pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and also the first time in history that it recorded two consecutive years of decline, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by economic activity also showed that economic activities in the vast majority of sectors recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracting more severely than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP started to rebound from the third quarter of 2020, ending the declines of the preceding five consecutive quarters (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption resumed positive growth in the third and fourth quarters; however, consumer sentiment remained weak as the authorities reimposed social distancing measures amid the third and fourth waves of the local epidemic. Overall investment expenditure also grew in the second half of the year alongside a brief improvement in business sentiment. Partly benefiting from the stronger performance of exports (especially exports to Mainland China), Hong Kong's merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). Services trade remained weak as global tourism was still at a standstill. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) dragged down GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting that the rebound in goods exports was slower than that of imports. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports To cope with the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two more rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund totaling $30.4 billion between September and December 2020 to help sectors and citizens affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021-22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and the provision of a 100% guaranteed personal special loan scheme for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced in March 2021 that the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme would be further extended to October of the same year, and announced the extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines expected to help economic activities return to normal, the Hong Kong economy is projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (as a whole), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, such as the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in the early part of 2021.
