On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, which will provide support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their mass vaccination programs, thereby affecting Hong Kong's merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2021 to range between 3.5% and 5.5%, while the growth forecasts by international organizations and private sector analysts average 4.4%. Labor market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17-year high (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. Total employment stabilized after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while Government figures showed that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal index of payroll per person engaged, which reflects labor earnings, saw its growth slow to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. To address the continuously deteriorating labor market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain employees. Following the end of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support sectors hard-hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 explores the potential impact of the boom and bust of inbound tourism on the local labor market. Chart 3.3 Labor market conditions Chart 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation Domestic inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell noticeably to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further dropped to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). The annualized three-month rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, remained at a low level despite some fluctuations in recent months. Specifically, price pressures on basic food eased, and the cost of meals bought away from home decreased visibly, reflecting that more restaurants offered takeaway discounts while dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures on other tradable goods (such as durable goods) remained moderate. As for services, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index remained soft alongside the consolidation of private housing rentals (Chart 3.5). Labor cost pressures also moderated in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 Rental component of the Composite CPI and market rentals Chart 3.6 Unit labor cost As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, domestic inflationary pressures should stay mild in the near term. In particular, domestic inflation will continue to be contained by the slower growth in newly signed private housing rentals earlier on. The market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate for 2021 to be at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate and headline inflation rate for 2021 to be 1% and 1.6% respectively. As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism quickly fell into a depression, raising market concerns that this crisis would cause scarring effects on the future recovery of the labor market. To this end, this Box empirically analyzes the impact of the inbound tourism boom on the local labor market, thereby exploring the potential implications of the current tourism depression. Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced significant booms and busts (Chart B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) epidemic in 2003. Following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year, visitor arrivals began to surge. Under the initial IVS, Mainland residents could apply in their individual capacity for one or two visits to Hong Kong per year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for a multiple-entry IVS endorsement valid for one year (multiple-entry permit). Since then, the number of Mainland visitor arrivals has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure connecting with Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached a record high between late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved the number of visitor arrivals in the second half of 2019, and amid the COVID-19 pandemic, inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies Using the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example, we explore the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We consider the introduction of the IVS in 2003 to be akin to a random economic shock, as it was largely exogenous in timing and its rollout could not be anticipated by Hong Kong citizens. Our main analytical data are drawn from the demographic data in the Hong Kong Population Census or By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% sample datasets from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. In addition, we define tourism-related sectors as the food and beverage, retail, hotel, and transportation sectors. First, we adopt a "difference-in-differences" analytical framework to compare the differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers (aged 20-40) in the "treatment group" and older workers (aged 41-65) in the "comparison group". We assign the younger cohort to the "treatment group" because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth of inbound tourism. Since the labor market impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS may change over time, we also employ an "event study" approach to identify the time-varying effects. Our empirical findings show that compared with the older cohort, younger workers (especially females and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related sectors after the implementation of the IVS. Among them, the impact of the IVS on the probability of young females working in tourism-related sectors was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at a level of nearly 5 percentage points (in terms of the average difference in entry probability compared with the older cohort) since 2006 (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar method to compare the earnings of those working in tourism-related sectors (treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related sectors (comparison group). The estimation results show that after the implementation of the IVS, the earnings growth of workers in tourism-related sectors was higher than that of employees in non-tourism-related sectors. Furthermore, compared with similar employees in other sectors, female workers and less-educated workers in tourism-related sectors experienced even higher earnings growth with an upward trend (3-20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the earnings of female and less-educated workers The above results are broadly in line with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, females, and less-educated workers. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analytical results, namely that the strong growth of inbound tourism increased the market demand for lower-skilled workers, improving the robustness of the labor market for the lower-skilled segment. As inbound tourism plunges from a boom to a trough, these groups of workers may be more affected, which warrants close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to trade close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, and the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that from robust initial public offering (IPO) fund-raising activities and southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates softened across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the ongoing Sino-US tensions may exacerbate the volatility of capital flows, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, making it capable of withstanding the pressures brought by volatile capital flows. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate trading close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that from robust IPO fund-raising activities and southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some of the funds raised from IPOs were repatriated, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range between 7.7505 and 7.7544 in November and December, due to the improved sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of increased funding demand towards the year-end. With fund-raising activities remaining active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar closed at 7.7568 on 26 February 2021. Overall, trading of the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, reflecting substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). For the whole year of 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times, with cumulative inflows amounting to HK$383.5 billion. Analyzed from a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits indicates that there were no signs of significant capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, without showing any abnormal capital movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar generally fell in tandem with the softening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and had a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the movement of the real effective exchange rate index largely tracked that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the ongoing Sino-US tensions may exacerbate the volatility of capital flows. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fund-raising activities (such as IPOs), resulting in substantial capital flowing in and out of the city. On the one hand, such fund-raising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, the funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business needs. Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, making it capable of withstanding the volatility of capital flows without compromising financial stability. Amid continuous capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. During the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base expanded by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). Analyzed by its components, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the expansion of the Aggregate Balance driven by the multiple triggerings of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking. On the other hand, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large-scale IPO fund-raising activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits generated by IPO subscription loans; therefore, the broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component rose significantly between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the conclusion of the IPO fund-raising activities and the repayment of IPO subscription loans by customers, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. Entering January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased substantially again, mainly driven by large-scale IPO fund-raising activities in late January. Overall, during the seven-month period since the end of June, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of the IPO fund-raising activities in late January, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. Analyzed by counterpart assets and excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the Monetary Base driven by the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (Chart 4.7). As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% during the same period; excluding the impact of the IPO fund-raising activities in late January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits recorded a decline due to low deposit interest rates, this was fully offset by the rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, which was partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets Total foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% during the seven-month period since the end of June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% during the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, due to the short-term volatility in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO fund-raising activities, total deposits with authorized institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the IPO fund-raising activities in late January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that as monthly monetary statistics may be subject to volatility driven by various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), these statistics should be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates generally remained at extremely low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite the large-scale IPO fund-raising activities in the second half of 2020, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates did not experience significant volatility due to the abundant liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve largely tracked the movement of the US dollar yield curve and steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% during the same period. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average interest rate for newly approved mortgage loans Hong Kong dollar interest rates at the retail level mainly declined in tandem with Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). Due to the lower funding costs, the average interest rate for newly approved mortgage loans also dropped from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, largely tracking the movement of the 1-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. On the other hand, the best lending rates of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given that US interest rates are expected to remain low for a prolonged period, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should continue to stay at low levels, with occasional fluctuations driven by capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, the abundant liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffers to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar have strengthened since the end of May (Chart 4.10), largely reflecting the better economic outlook of Mainland China compared to the rest of the world, as well as the weakness of the US dollar. FTSE Russell's announcement in late September to include Mainland government bonds in its World Government Bond Index further supported the strengthening of the renminbi through investment demand. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium over the onshore renminbi exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards the year-end, it remained below 4% for most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fell in tandem with onshore renminbi interest rates in late December, and subsequently rose again in late January, partly due to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fixings In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued its growth trend. Since the fourth quarter, the growth of renminbi deposits has accelerated, reflecting to some extent the appreciation of the renminbi and its higher interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a faster pace, reaching RMB 826.3 billion at the end of January 2021, representing an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among this, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by the strong growth in corporate customer deposits. On the other hand, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit decreased by 25.0% during the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong As for other renminbi business, the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB 159.2 billion during the seven-month period since the end of June 2020. On the other hand, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven months from July 2020 to January 2021, the value of transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong reached RMB 3,769.5 billion, an increase of 16.7% compared with the same period last year. Among these transactions, the growth of remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland was higher than that of remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong has a massive renminbi liquidity pool, which is sufficient to continue supporting a large volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. For the whole year of 2020, the average daily turnover of the renminbi RTGS system reached RMB 1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB 1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Due to the persistent economic recession caused by the recurring COVID-19 pandemic, coupled with the impact of a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong further declined in the second half of 2020, and asset quality also slightly deteriorated. Nevertheless, given their still-strong capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust. During the review period, to continue supporting the overall economy in tiding over the difficulties, the HKMA decided to extend various relief measures. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions will be detrimental to business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic will weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. As a result, the return on assets dropped to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared to 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), causing a decrease in net interest income that more than offset the slight growth in non-interest income, leading to a decline in profitability. For the full year of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the return on assets decreased from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely driven by massive fund inflows associated with stock market activities, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Among them, the 3-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The trend of the Composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) was broadly similar, dropping significantly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the Composite interest rate mainly reflected the decrease in interbank funding costs and the downward adjustment of time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks Looking ahead, as the global low-interest-rate environment is highly likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' net interest margin performance, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging. Furthermore, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the considerable uncertainties surrounding the distribution and efficacy of vaccines. The aforementioned risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. The capitalization of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, higher than the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio during the period was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum level of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated AIs Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratio figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirement also indicated that the funding positions of AIs were stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of Category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of Category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75% respectively. The ample liquidity and robust funding positions of AIs demonstrated that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the major source of funding for AIs, reflecting that the banking system maintained a stable funding structure. At the end of 2020, the proportion of customer deposits to the total liabilities of all AIs hovered at 56.1%, similar to the level six months ago (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all AIs As the total deposits of all AIs increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans decreased during the same period, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs across all currencies fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. As a result, as of the end of 2020, the average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively, compared to 86.4% and 65.5% respectively six months ago. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Assuming a shock of a 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks was estimated to be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of a persistent economic recession caused by the recurring pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances experienced a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for the full year of 2020, total credit of the banking sector still recorded positive growth, although the growth pace slowed significantly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all AIs, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was due to decreases in both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Among them, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half of the year, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared to their respective growths of 2.6% and 4.2% in the preceding six-month period. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Analyzed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans, after decreasing by 2.0% in the first half of the year, remained broadly at a level similar to that at the end of June by the end of 2020. Foreign currency loans, after surging by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decline in demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector turned slightly more optimistic about the short-term credit demand outlook compared to six months ago. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed AIs expecting an increase in loan demand over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting a decrease in loan demand over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment ability of households and corporates, the loan quality of banks slightly deteriorated, but remained robust by historical and international standards. In addition, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed down in the second half of 2020. The total classified loan ratio of all AIs rose moderately from 0.79% six months ago to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all AIs increased from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. For retail banks, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economy performed sluggishly, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify across various regions, particularly in the US. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale pandemic outbreaks, and if US inflation is more persistent and broad-based than expected, the tightening of monetary policy may exceed expectations. If the US Federal Reserve significantly tightens monetary policy and causes global financial conditions to tighten, it will exert pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could bring significant impacts to the global economy through trade and financial channels, and further complicate the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, and there were no notable signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For the whole year of 2021, the growth of total bank loans accelerated somewhat. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened somewhat since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the sustained economic recovery. Coupled with the potentially faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalization, these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow down in late 2021, and the weakness extended into 2022, as the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant led to increased global mobility restrictions, coupled with persistent supply bottlenecks that weighed on production. Meanwhile, amid supply-demand imbalances and labor shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have broadened to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies (especially the US). Recently, with the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, the surge in commodity prices could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility may lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, complicating the global monetary policy outlook. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a massive shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turbulence, some open-ended funds suffered massive capital outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Capital outflows from selected open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode In addition to investors' liquidity needs, another reason for the massive capital outflows could be investors taking a "first-mover advantage" to redeem funds early, thereby avoiding the redemption costs that could spike under market stress. To curb capital outflows driven by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopt swing pricing—an open-ended fund pricing rule that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, there is no empirical research indicating whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this background, this feature conducts an empirical study to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce capital outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby lowering their liquidity risks. In addition, this feature will also identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during market stress. Based on these assessments, we will put forward policy recommendations regarding financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby passing the redemption costs onto them. The first-mover advantage mainly exists in open-ended funds that adopt traditional pricing rules, where the subscription and redemption costs of the fund's investors (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund's price after the transactions are executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not have to bear these transaction costs. This creates an incentive for them to redeem funds early, especially when large redemption costs are expected. Therefore, during market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced as redemption costs are expected to rise. This amplifies the redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by open-ended funds.

Major global stock markets continued to rally in the fourth quarter of 2021, but have consolidated since January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong stock market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, mainly dragged down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding pandemic developments in Hong Kong caused the Hang Seng Index to fall to a near two-year low at the end of February. Meanwhile, the offshore RMB bond market in Hong Kong continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weakened asset market sentiment and a new wave of local pandemic outbreaks. Major global stock markets generally continued to rally in the last quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI All Country World Index to hit a record high of 3,262 on January 4, 2022 (Chart 4.11). Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings supported the upward trend of major global stock markets, although the pandemic remained a major risk concern for investors throughout the year. However, major global stock markets have consolidated since early January 2022, as the market became increasingly concerned about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, soaring commodity prices, and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. In contrast, at the end of 2021, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag behind other major global stock markets. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 from September to mid-November, and closed at 23,398 at the end of 2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, value investors' buying interest returned to the Hong Kong stock market, driving the Hang Seng Index to rebound to around 25,000 in January. However, uncertainties surrounding pandemic developments in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index down to a near two-year low of 22,713 at the end of February. Throughout the review period from the end of August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI All Country World Index dropped by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). The profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio rose slightly in the second half of 2021, but it remained at a low level by historical and international standards. Backed by robust capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, to further assist the economy in weathering the difficult times, the HKMA extended various support measures. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the economic recovery, which, coupled with the risk of a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalization, will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 16.1% compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profitability was mainly driven by decreases in net interest and non-interest income, as well as an increase in operating expenses. Consequently, the return on assets fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.1). For the full year of 2021, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while the return on assets declined from 0.77% to 0.59%. However, given that liquidity in the banking system remained highly abundant, interbank rates continued to stay at low levels. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose slightly by 9 basis points from six months ago to 0.26% at the end of December 2021 (see the blue line in Chart 5.3). The funding costs of retail banks remained stable during the review period. Although the normalization of US monetary policy may herald an improvement in banks' profitability, the short-term improvement may be partially offset by two factors. First, despite the Federal Reserve indicating multiple interest rate hikes in 2022, past experience shows that movements in local interest rates may lag behind US interest rates (especially when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains highly abundant). Therefore, the improvement in banks' net interest margins may take more time to materialize. Furthermore, the surge in Omicron variant cases may also introduce uncertainties to the pace of economic recovery, thereby putting pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability. Climate change affects every aspect of our lives, and everyone has a responsibility to play a part in mitigating its impact. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted significant efforts to advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and contributing to the enhancement of global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our inaugural sustainability report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021 last year, we are publishing the Sustainability Report 2022 as a standalone document for the first time this year. I hope this report will provide readers with a deeper understanding of the HKMA's strategies and priorities in strengthening the climate resilience of Hong Kong's banking system, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our roles as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability initiatives across the HKMA's major functions. You will find details of our specific measures and work in this report, with the key highlights as follows: Banks face climate risks in their day-to-day operations. As a banking regulator, the HKMA has taken specific measures to strengthen banks' climate resilience. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into our supervisory processes, and explored how to harness the power of technology to assist banks in assessing the impact of physical risks. In view of the increasing number of green and sustainable products launched by banks, we also shared good practices with the industry on the proper management of these products to facilitate banks in strengthening their climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives on addressing climate risks and promoting the development of sustainable finance. Domestically, we are collaborating with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green taxonomy framework; this framework will enhance transparency in the financial markets and bring greater alignment to green finance policies. At the international level, we are actively participating in various international organisations to assist in formulating policies to address climate change and assessing its impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet the demand for green and sustainable financing in Asia. Although 2022 was a highly challenging year for the global bond market, the amount of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong continued to record strong growth, increasing by 42% to reach a total of US$80.5 billion, making it the largest centre in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². These issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government and the Hainan Provincial People's Government, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the international market. The flourishing development of Hong Kong's green bond market is also partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing nearly US$16 billion worth of green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation, among others. We also assisted the Government in achieving two "firsts", including the issuance of the inaugural batch of government green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion in May 2022, which was the largest green retail bond issuance globally at the time. In addition, we assisted the Government in issuing the inaugural batch of tokenised green bonds in February 2023. This was the world's first batch of tokenised green bonds issued by a government, and the issuance marked a significant milestone in successfully combining our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech. Standards, data and talent are indispensable elements for driving the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and their establishment relies on the efforts and collaboration across different sectors. To this end, the HKMA collaborates with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry, primarily through the Steering Group, to develop these elements. In addition to the aforementioned development of the local green taxonomy framework, the Steering Group also promotes capacity building in the industry and enhances Hong Kong's data resources through the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance established under its auspices. Furthermore, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas such as the mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund's responsible investment efforts, in particular by setting a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Meanwhile, we also enhanced our risk management practices to improve the Exchange Fund's climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. In addition, to fully capitalise on the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to driving the Exchange Fund's sustainable investments, seeking out investment opportunities that support climate transition and mitigate climate change, thereby enhancing the long-term returns of the investment portfolio. At the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared to the 2017 level. In fact, the Exchange Fund's exposure to highly carbon-intensive assets has consistently remained lower than that of the broader market. Going forward, we will continue to advance towards our net-zero emissions target by continuously strengthening the integration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into our investment management process, actively exercising active ownership, continuously collaborating with various stakeholders, and focusing on the decarbonisation and transition of our investment portfolio. Within the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built upon three main pillars: environment, staff and social responsibility. On the environmental front, we are committed to fostering a green working environment and promoting a more environmentally friendly market to the public; on the staff front, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively cultivate a healthy and inclusive working environment; and on the social responsibility front, we are committed to enhancing public financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion and actively giving back to the community. Compared to the levels when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper consumption in 2022 all achieved double-digit percentage reductions. More importantly, we have formulated a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by or before 2050. In the short term, our target is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and, using 2015 as the baseline, reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by or before 2030. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require continuous efforts and collaboration from multiple parties. On this critical global issue, we recognise the need to walk the talk, lead by example, and work alongside like-minded peers and international organisations. In the next section, we will outline the HKMA's short-term plans and key priorities in addressing climate change across our major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by or before 2050 is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort in attaining this goal. We are confident that with the concerted efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the wider community, we will be able to successfully navigate the climate challenges ahead. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong's financial industry and fulfill its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable organization. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organizations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the regulator of the banking sector, we will strive to enhance the climate resilience of the banking industry and further improve our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will communicate with banks to understand their progress in implementing regulatory requirements for climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the Common Assessment Framework on "Greenness Baseline" for the banking sector. At the same time, the HKMA will support banks in their efforts to enhance climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as exploring different measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure, and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress testing as part of the regular supervisor-driven stress testing for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their climate risk resilience based on an enhanced stress testing framework, which covers multiple stress scenarios including extreme weather and adverse economic environments. To promote the healthy development of banks in providing green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on the selling process in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site thematic reviews to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to strengthen the building of the green finance ecosystem to support the green transition of the financial industry, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of developing a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the issuance size of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and enlarging the scope of the Programme to cover sustainable bonds; at the same time, it will attract more green financing activities to be conducted in Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA is also assisting in the implementation of the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme to expand Hong Kong's talent pool for green finance. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions, and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance and technology. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other agencies and departments through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sectoral issues such as capacity building and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly launch various specific initiatives with the International Finance Corporation in the Asian region, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks develop roadmaps to make green finance a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership program to expand the Alliance's influence in the Asian region. At the same time, the Alliance will also step up efforts to enhance the professional capacity of industry practitioners, promote green finance knowledge sharing, and lead the launch of project initiatives in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target to achieve net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio by or before 2050, as its commitment to participating in global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to integrate environmental, social, and governance factors into its investment management process, strive towards the net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organization, the HKMA cares about its staff as well as the general public and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as our commitment to participating in global decarbonization and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritize the reduction of carbon emissions and encourage staff to fully support energy conservation and waste reduction. In addition, we will provide further guidance to staff to incorporate sustainability principles into the procurement process. To implement digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernize internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency, while minimizing potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process as much as possible.

Climate change is a major risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening the Hong Kong financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals as well as the global sustainable development agenda. Banks face the impact of various sustainability and climate-related issues in their daily business operations. To continue performing their vital functions in the financial system and to channel more funds into green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places special emphasis on building banks' capacity to address and manage climate risks, and accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 issued principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and published responses to frequently asked questions to clarify how the existing Basel framework covers these risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into the supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA has maintained communication with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress, and challenges in implementing the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks' climate risk management, the HKMA has formulated a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process, which was communicated to the banking industry in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the HKMA issued the revised SPM module SA-1 "Risk-based Supervisory Approach" and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risks into the risk-based supervisory process. Meanwhile, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress test scenarios and assessment framework based on the experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise. The HKMA also formulated plans to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into the regular supervisor-driven stress testing, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector's resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its Greenness Assessment Framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Meanwhile, the HKMA is reviewing the Supervisory Review Process used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, aiming to encourage banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing popularity of green and sustainable products issued by banks, the HKMA conducted a round of thematic reviews focusing on banks' development and ongoing management of these products. The HKMA identified some good practices during the thematic reviews and issued a circular in December to share them with the industry, facilitating banks to progressively enhance their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and enhance banks' capabilities in managing climate risks. The HKMA has commenced the development of a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and supervisory authorities, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub to explore how technological solutions can assist in conducting physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering practices; this work adopts advanced analytics and compliance technology, supplemented by fully automated supervisory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the anti-money laundering supervisory data collection process to reduce the manual burden on banks and paper consumption. To enhance transparency across financial markets and align green finance policies more closely, the HKMA collaborated with other financial regulators to develop a local green classification framework. The green classification framework, commonly known as a green taxonomy, classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained engagement with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to delve into the features and challenges of the framework, and is preparing to propose and consult on the structure and core elements of the framework in the first half of 2023. The HKMA is well aware that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, and has therefore incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen ongoing surveillance work. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its continuous monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analysis of climate-related risks in various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Workstream on Scenario Design and Analysis under the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA assists in further enriching climate scenarios, enabling central banks and supervisors to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. On the research front, the HKMA conducted several applied research projects in 2022, delving into two major topics, namely greenwashing behaviour in the corporate green bond market3, and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures4. The findings of the above research help formulate policies and supervisory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared the research findings with various stakeholders through multiple channels, including international central bank research conferences and the HKMA's Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA's Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralised standby liquidity arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is exploring the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps facilitate international and regional policy dialogues on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, and draws insights from them to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA has stepped up its efforts to enhance market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and catalysts, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the financial sector's response to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the growth of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government's climate strategies1. The Steering Group's work is primarily guided by its strategic plan, which sets out six key focus areas and five action points to strengthen Hong Kong's financial ecosystem for a greener and more sustainable future (Chart 1). Strengthening climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong's position as a global risk management centre; promoting the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection; enhancing the relevant skills of industry practitioners and raising public awareness; encouraging product innovation and research initiatives to channel capital towards green and sustainable projects; capitalizing on the business opportunities presented by the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance centre in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA); and strengthening regional and international cooperation. Actions taken to date to advance sustainable finance development in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. The Steering Group's current priorities include capacity building and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), a green taxonomy (see "Building a green classification framework to facilitate green capital flows" in the "Building a Sustainable Financial System" chapter on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, the Steering Group published a preliminary feasibility assessment of carbon market opportunities for Hong Kong in March, and will support the development of Hong Kong into a regional carbon trading centre, including the development of a high-quality international voluntary carbon market and capitalizing on opportunities arising from GBA cooperation. In December, the Steering Group announced a partnership with CDP2 to enhance data availability and sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of this collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which not only facilitates sustainability reporting by companies, but also assists financial institutions in collecting and analyzing company-level data for risk assessment and relevant business decisions. This is a significant step forward in expanding the coverage of the Steering Group's data work to include SMEs, a crucial segment of the economy that was previously difficult to reach. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to coordinate the efforts of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions in capacity building and policy formulation, and to build a repository of resources and data. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three repositories focusing on data, training information and internship opportunities respectively, to help the financial industry and other sectors access data and learning resources related to green and sustainable finance. The repositories provide data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong. To facilitate industry talent training, the Centre assisted the Government in launching the Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme in December, providing subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates participating in training and upskilling related to green and sustainable finance. Other initiatives to promote capacity building include the launch of the Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative to create more internship opportunities for students, and the development of a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module under the HKMA's Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners3. "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme" The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the HKMA launched the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks4, bringing together financial institutions, banking industry associations, research institutions and innovative technology providers in the region to jointly develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realize their potential in mainstreaming green finance as a core business, and to promote the financial system's participation in global climate change-related activities. Its mode of operation provides a one-stop mutual learning platform for financial institutions to acquire the necessary knowledge, tools and information to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions; brings together green finance leaders to connect green financial institutions across different emerging markets; facilitates communication and explores frontier issues; and drives the global green finance agenda to unlock endless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five leading global financial institutions5 became cornerstone members of the Alliance, working closely with the IFC and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities to help achieve the transition to a green economy. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner6 committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardization to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone members, the IFC and the HKMA signed a memorandum of understanding. On the other hand, since March 2021, the Alliance has held 18 training events and roundtables, attracting over 6,000 participants from across the globe, including the Asia-Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. Furthermore, in June 2022, the Alliance, together with the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)7, published its first frontier issue research report titled "Climate Risk: Definitions, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulatory Oversight". The HKMA has been promoting green and sustainable debt issuance and building a local ecosystem of related professional services. The total amount of green and sustainable debt (including bonds and loans) issued in Hong Kong in 2022 reached US$80.5 billion, an increase of 42%. +42% Green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion). To demonstrate the Government's commitment to combating climate change, promoting green finance and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and livable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the implementation of the relevant green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued close to US$16 billion equivalent of green institutional and retail bonds, with the proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the Programme, the Government publishes a Green Bond Report annually, detailing the allocation of green bond proceeds and their expected environmental benefits. To allow the public to participate in and share the fruits of Hong Kong's sustainable development through investment, the inaugural batch of green retail bonds worth HK$20 billion was issued in May. It received enthusiastic support from the public and became the largest green retail bond issuance globally at the time. This issuance also expanded the variety of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong, consolidating its position as a premier regional and international green finance hub. The Government also continued its regular green institutional bond issuances in the 2022-23 financial year, issuing US$5.75 billion equivalent of green bonds in January 2023. This triple-currency offering, covering US dollars, euros and renminbi with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continues to provide an important benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in the Government's previous green bond issuances, reflecting investors' strong confidence in Hong Kong's long-term credit fundamentals and economic underlying conditions. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi tranches to RMB 10 billion. The share of international investors and Mainland investors participating in the issuance through Southbound Trading under Bond Connect also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong's status as the premier offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating its leadership position as an international financial centre. The HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing tokenized institutional green bonds in February 2023 to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This was the first batch of tokenized green bonds issued by a government globally. This primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis on a private blockchain network, and subsequent processes (including coupon payments, secondary market trade settlement and maturity redemption) were also digitized. The experience gained from this government issuance can provide a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future. To provide credible and convenient market information to the industry, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region respectively. The report by the International Capital Market Association showed that Hong Kong became the largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bonds in Asia in 2022, with the total amount of bonds arranged in Hong Kong reaching US$27.8 billion, accounting for over one-third of the regional total. The largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bonds in Asia US$27.8 billion Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government issued another RMB 5 billion of offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB 2.6 billion of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the People's Government of Hainan Province also issued RMB 5 billion of offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, including blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances once again highlight Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring status as the premier fundraising platform in the region. The HKMA continued to promote and administer the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme launched in 2021, leveraging the scheme to attract more related professional service providers (including financial institutions, green advisory firms and external reviewers) to establish and expand their businesses in Hong Kong. The scheme has been well received by the industry. As of the end of 2022, the scheme had covered the pre-issuance, post-issuance or both external review service expenses for over 180 green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. Starting from March, the scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan size threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, helping smaller enterprises obtain green financing. Following the successful completion of the proof-of-concept for tokenized retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre collaborated again under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitized carbon forwards (also known as Mitigation Outcome Interests, or MOIs), thereby enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental integrity of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that use blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitized MOIs.

As one of the world's largest asset owners and managers, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) plays an important role in promoting green and sustainable finance development to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment, having taken the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets as early as 2015. It requires its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership issued by the Securities and Futures Commission, and integrates environmental, social, and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently in accordance with the principle of "capital preservation first, long-term growth next", believing that emphasizing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate related risks. Facing the increasingly severe challenges of climate change, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting a "Net-Zero by 2050" target in 2022 and optimizing its risk management strategy to enhance the resilience of its asset portfolio, thereby striving for better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to jointly promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organizations to formulate ESG investment standards. The transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risks. To fulfill its commitment to supporting the Glasgow Declaration published by the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 UN Climate Change Conference and to greening the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee (EFAC), chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office (EFIO) in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is for the HKMA to prioritize ESG investments with comparable risk-adjusted long-term returns to other projects, in order to align with the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the HKMA's responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website: The Investment Sub-Committee under EFAC, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for monitoring the ESG and climate-related risks involved in the Exchange Fund's investments. The Investment Sub-Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors the progress of integrating ESG factors into investments and the ESG profile of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Division of the EFIO. As shown in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established under the EFIO, chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is responsible for coordinating and monitoring various ESG initiatives within the EFIO. The initiatives and work progress discussed at each meeting of the ESG Committee are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the EFIO.
